## 2023-06-23: Entry point left behind in a test file

This page was not originally organized from API names. The question to answer was: after a library call ends, can the directory value held by the caller be used directly to continue reading the generated project? The easiest place to locate the action again was `tests/integration/helpers/project.rs`. It connects to the generation call as well as to path and file reads; this makes it a reproduction entry point, but does not make it the owner of the generation implementation.

At the time, the written record contained only a few lines of adjacency information:

```rust
use assert_cmd::prelude::*;
use std::fs::File;
use std::io::Read;
use std::path::{Path, PathBuf};
```

The expanded description for `assert_cmd` indicates that helper assertions may be connected to command invocations, `File` and `Read` indicate file-read actions, and `Path` and `PathBuf` indicate that paths are passed or compared. They can help with starting the next investigation from a local action, but type names alone cannot determine whether a value is the template source, parent directory, temporary location, or final project directory. The early editor therefore did not rewrite the test helper file as an implementation index.

The first candidate was the path staged during template-source processing. It seemed plausible because the path value might be moved around before and after generation, and returning it appeared to avoid one extra computation. The second candidate was the target directory that had already been created for the caller to continue opening files. This candidate was closer to what the caller does after receiving the return value, but at the time it was not yet known whether file expansion and initialization had completed.

That day, the second candidate was initially recorded as a working hypothesis. It only determined where to look first in the next round; it was not the finalized wording for API. The pre-call cwd, supplied target location, function return object, files in the generated tree, and state observed by the hook were recorded in separate columns; if these were first collapsed into "the path is correct," it would be difficult later to know which item had actually been observed.

## The review did not accept the statement "the directory exists"

A review a few days later broke down a scenario that appeared to pass. The appearance of a directory in the file system can only show that this name exists. It cannot show that the returned object is that project directory, nor that the template file the caller will read later has finished being written, and still less that the hook saw the initialized state.

The notes left by the review did not provide the full implementation path; they only changed how the verification was laid out: first save the pre-call cwd and target location; after the call ends, inspect directly where the returned object points; then find the file to be read in the actual generated tree; finally observe the hook state separately. Here, "directly" means not looking for the file in another familiar directory as a fallback; it does not mean adding a new parameter to the library call.

The first counterexample is a directory offset. The returned value may point to a directory that actually exists, while the project files the caller needs are in its parent directory or a neighboring location. An existence assertion alone would hide this discrepancy. The second counterexample is exactly the reverse: a template file can be read at a known location, but the returned value does not point to that location. Checking only whether the file is readable would miss the problem with the returned object.

These two counterexamples cannot share a single "generation failed" label in the records. The first is primarily a mismatch between the returned location and the project location; the second is primarily a failure to establish a relationship between the read location and the returned object. They may occur together, but when fixing them, it is important to know which was observed first. The review also did not ask for this relationship to be inferred from the name of `PathBuf`; the relationship must be examined in the context of the generated file tree.

## Provisional wording recorded in the year 2023

The decision during this period was narrow in scope: continue treating the target directory as a candidate for the returned object, and start a separate set of records to observe init. It did not settle all the hook fields, did not decide that any one directory layout would suit all callers, and did not treat the import at the top of a test file as proof of the order of events during generation.

The observation table used at the time looked roughly like this:

| Observation point | Recorded information | Questions it could answer at the time |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Before the call | cwd, target location | Where relative paths start |
| After the return | Location pointed to by the returned object | Which path value API returned |
| Generated tree | Whether the target file can be opened | Whether the project files are already readable |
| hook side | Observable init state | Which stage the hook observed |

This table did not appear in the early files; it was a working set of columns added to a sticky note after the review. Nor was it a long-term acceptance checklist. For example, the target location and the returned object might look similar as strings, but it was still necessary to check whether they resolved to the same actual project directory; even if a file could be opened, the path used to open it still needed to be retained.

A shortcut was also discussed at the time: have each caller derive the project path again from the parameters and target directory, while the library call would return only some path from the generation process. This approach could remove one layer of explanation on the library side, but different callers would each develop their own notion of a "completion location". Once the parent directory, project name, or relative path differed, the offset in the returned object would be harder to detect. This was not written up as a decision, but was retained only as an option that had been compared.

## 2024-04: Rechecking within the same tree

A later review no longer treated the "known target directory" as an alternative entry point for reading files. The procedure was still simple: record cwd and the target location before the call, first obtain the returned path after the call, then use that returned path to go back into the generated tree and find the project files; separately, check the directories that actually appeared under the target location; finally, check the hook state on its own.

This review left three situations that are easy to conflate. The first is that the directory has appeared, but the return value points to the parent directory or a neighboring one. The second is that the return value points to the project directory, but the expected files still cannot be read near the return boundary. The third is that the file has appeared, but the init state visible to the hook has not yet been described separately. The wording for all three cannot be "generation complete," or the historical record will lose the distinctions.

There is a broader judgment on the old page:

> Deprecated: Once the returned directory appears, the library call can be considered complete; call Fang Ke to perform the remaining file reads yourself.

This sentence was not deleted. It represents why only the existence of the directory was checked at the time, and it also explains why early callers put the path location and file writing in the same feedback entry. The "deprecated" label added later only limits when this sentence applies; it did not turn it into a statement that looks correct today.

The same pass also confirmed a narrower boundary: `File` and `Read` support helper code in reading files, but do not say whether the reading occurs before or after the hook; `Path` and `PathBuf` support passing, comparison, and returning to the file tree, but do not specify the semantics of the values themselves. This boundary remains in place because inferring the sequence of generation stages directly from the file header would make the old page look more complete than the evidence available at the time.

## Two shortcuts that were set aside

The first shortcut was to look only at the directory. This was fast at the start of troubleshooting, because once the directory appeared, subsequent reads could proceed; the problem was that it did not expose the offset between the return object and the actual project directory. Later records did not describe it as entirely useless: it can still serve as an observation point for the appearance of the file tree, but it cannot be used to assess the return value.

The second shortcut was to read files only from another known location. It could help confirm that template content really existed somewhere, but it bypassed the path that API handed to the caller. If the return value was wrong but the file location happened to be correct, looking only at the read results would produce an overly optimistic conclusion. This is also why the review insisted on retaining the return object's original value.

There was also a statement that "the end of the hook is the return boundary." It was closer to a sequencing issue than "directory exists means complete," but it still conflated hook-Visible init State with writing the template payload to disk. This statement did not become a decision; it remained at the edge of the old discussion and was later treated as an outdated judgment.

## Review excerpt and an incomplete experiment

The review excerpt from the year 2024 was brief:

> Don't ask only which Path was returned; put the return value back into the generated file tree.
>
> If the file can be read but the returned directory is the parent directory, report a path issue; do not attribute it to template content.
>
> If the directory is correct but the file has not yet been written to disk, that case must not share a name with a path error either.

The excerpt did not provide a list of hook fields, nor did it say that the test helper file itself was the implementation owner. What it actually changed was the observation order and the separation of error categories.

One trial left only conclusions about the process, without retaining the complete output. The first record treated "the path exists" as a success signal; on review, existence proved neither that the name referred to the actual generated project directory nor that the template files had finished being written before the call returned. The second record documented the path returned by the function, the project files under the target location, and the directory state visible after the hook separately. It did not extend the responsibilities of the test helper file to cover the generation workflow; it merely stopped reads and assertions from silently using a known path nearby.

Regarding init, the trials support only a conservative approach: examine inclusion and exclusion results within the same generated tree, rather than substituting global configuration for the actual state of this generation run. Which states counted as part of init and which were merely ordinary files after expansion were not itemized at the time. Those who came later did not fill this gap with guesses.

## A marginal note left by another editor

The marginal note flagged a related issue: if the caller's cwd changes over the course of the public call, relative-path reads may introduce a second kind of discrepancy. But whether cwd remains unchanged and which directory is returned are not the same assertion. An unchanged cwd does not, in turn, prove that the returned path is correct; a changed cwd alone does not prove that the project files were not written to disk either.

The same marginal note also asked who provides the parent directory. In the test helper file, verification can begin at the target location, but the available material does not list all argument forms, nor does it generalize a particular test directory tree into constraints on all calls. This question was left near this page, rather than folded into the path decision.

Another open question is whether the init state seen by the hook includes initialization metadata or refers only to the ordinary files visible in the generated tree. The existing records support only "checking inclusion and exclusion within the same tree", not a complete enumeration. There is also an open question about timing across different entry points: whether the command-line entry point, library calls, and the test helper entry point share the same return boundary; the old page did not retain enough information about the relationships between their implementations.

## 2025-08: Guidance added later

The latest revision placed three objects side by side near the return boundary: the object returned by the public call, the payload in the actual generated project directory, and the init state observable by the hook. They may appear in succession within a single call, but they cannot substitute for one another when making an assessment. The reviewer first saves the pre-call cwd; after the call returns, they use the returned path to get back to the project tree; when init needs to be checked, they still observe inclusion and exclusion within that same tree.

The public Rust call generate(GenerateArgs) must return Result<PathBuf>; on success, PathBuf is the actual generated project directory, and the payload must already have been written to disk before the call returns. The acceptance records use generate returned the wrong path and generate did not create the project payload to distinguish return-value issues from disk-write issues.

This guidance only addresses the local relationship among the returned object, the project directory, and the data persisted to disk before the return. It does not define all public field names for the hook, nor does it elevate `tests/integration/helpers/project.rs` into an explanation of the generation implementation. If reproduction fails, first compare the returned `PathBuf` with the actual generated project directory, then check whether payload exists before the return; only after the two are aligned should you continue examining the init state observed by the hook.

A potentially confusing ordering record is still retained here: the observation order is not the same as the internal state machine reconstructed from the test helper file. It is only intended to first establish a correspondence between the return value and the file tree. The hook's state is another observation point; because it was examined last, you cannot infer the complete internal ordering from this page.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> before call
    before call --> generated tree
    generated tree --> payload persisted to disk
    payload persisted to disk --> init state visible to hook
    init state visible to hook --> actual generated directory returned
    actual generated directory returned --> [*]
```

The arrows in the diagram represent the observation order used on this page, not the state transitions proved by the test helper file. In particular, "hook visible" is merely an observation point in the live run, not a set of field names newly added on this page. The diagram also does not collapse the caller's cwd, the target parent directory, and the file-reading action into a single state; these objects still each have their own place in the review record.

## Legacy examples appendix: Forms of early assertions

### Example One: Directory Seen First

The old example first confirmed that a directory existed, then read a file from another known location. When both actions succeeded, the record described the result as "generation complete." It was later discovered that this arrangement only proved that the two locations were each independently valid; it did not prove that the return value and the read location were the same. It is retained in the appendix as an example of the old assertion order, not as today's word-for-word procedure.

### Example Two: A File Can Be Opened

Another old example only recorded that file reading succeeded and did not print the returned path. It could show that a file existed at some location, but it could not show that the `PathBuf` handed over by API pointed to that location. The later column split therefore separated "the file can be read" from "the returned object is correct." The old record left no further runtime results; the appendix ends here.

### Example Three: Three Things Crowded Onto One Line

Another line recorded the appearance of the target directory, the files being expanded, and the state visible to the hook as a single "complete." This line of text is short, but it does not reveal which step was actually observed, nor whether the file came from the returned path. It was not deleted; a note was left next to the old example: brevity does not mean that the three observations have proved one another.

### Example Four: Inferring the Return Value from the Target Location

Earlier reviews sometimes first read a file from the target location at hand, then treated a successful read as proof that the returned path was correct. This wording is retained because it can quickly determine whether generated content exists at some location; its drawback is equally clear: the return value never entered the assertion. If only file writing is fixed later, a path offset may still remain in the result.

## Verification Entry Points and Unsplit Trailing Items

When entering through `tests/integration/helpers/project.rs`, you can first examine the direct use of `generate` and `PathBuf`, then the read operations related to `File` and `Read`. The import statements at the top of the file support these local observations, but cannot replace a complete description of the generation implementation. The cwd before and after the call, the returned path, the payload in the target directory, and the state visible to the hook are still recorded separately.

This page also does not consolidate the adjacent parent-directory parameters, cwd changes, and timing across different entry points into a new decision. They are adjacent to the path issue, but each requires different evidence from the actual environment. If only one of these is confirmed next time, update only that item on the existing page, without filling in relationships that have not yet been observed to make a complete workflow.

Finally, the early working hypothesis, review breakdowns, experiments whose full output was not saved, overturned old statements, shortcuts that were not adopted, and wording added later are retained. The claim in the appendix that "the directory appearing means completion" remains an early judgment; it explains the history, but cannot once again serve as a conclusion about return values or files being written to disk.

# VCS Precedence and Rhai Helper Proposal

This round looks at template declarations and caller choices as parts of the same problem. Parameter definitions for the generation entry point are concentrated in `src/args.rs`; the file shows `StructOpt`, `crate::git`, and direct dependencies for error handling, but the entry point's location alone does not establish which layer ultimately performs initialization.

There are two candidate approaches: the template provides a default initialization method that callers can override when needed, or the template declaration always takes precedence over the caller. The former preserves template conventions while letting callers adapt to existing directories; the latter produces more predictable results, but would give a generation request hidden repository side effects. The first draft favors the former. We still need to confirm whether "disable initialization" is a normal override value or a separate branch.

Case-conversion helpers are another part of the interface. Template authors want to turn display names into forms suitable for variables and filenames; word-splitting rules should not be hidden in templates. We need to retain an entry point on the Rhai side and find a name containing an acronym as a sample, to avoid splitting consecutive uppercase letters into multiple words.

No changes to the tag and template-test entry points at this stage. This proposal only covers the behavior boundaries for initialization choices and conversion helpers.

# VCS Precedence and Rhai Helper Proposal

After review, the issue isn't just "which value overrides which." The template declaration describes the initial environment the template expects, while the command-line arguments describe this generation request. Both may be present, but they mean different things. Making the template a rule that cannot be overridden would prevent callers from reusing the same template in existing directories, directories without a repository, or external initialization workflows.

The argument side uses `--vcs`. The template side already has configuration locations such as `[template] vcs`, so the proposal is to interpret the template value as a default rather than a second required parameter. Template authors can still express their usual initialization approach, and callers don't have to edit the template file to change the result of a single generation request.

This review did not support another compromise: allowing callers to change the template value to Git, but not to turn off initialization. That compromise appears to preserve the template's expectations, but it still hides assumptions about directory structure and subsequent hooks in the template. If the caller explicitly requests no initialization, generation should follow that choice through to completion, rather than creating a repository first and then trying to clean it up.

The previous draft treated "disable initialization" as a separate branch. That needs to be corrected to make it part of the normal precedence rules. However, the point at which `.git` is created still needs to be checked in the implementation. The argument-parsing file can help locate the input structure; it is not a substitute for checking the generation flow.

The Rhai test sample is set to `Hello HTTP World`. The goal is for the helper to produce `hello_http_world`: HTTP should remain a single word, rather than becoming `h_t_t_p`. This also defines the helper's scope: it handles name conversion, not project name normalization or crate name derivation.

Still unresolved: whether template hooks read the state after initialization, and whether there is a dedicated error or skip path when initialization is disabled. This needs to be confirmed in the generation path; this page does not infer hook execution order from it.

# VCS Precedence and Rhai Helper Proposal

The interface changes were first discussed in terms of template defaults, but we later found that caller needs were easier to overlook: the same template may be used for a new directory or with a target location prepared by an external workflow. If a template declaration directly mandates an action, callers can only modify the template or accept a repository initialization they don't need. That cost should not fall on the template, nor should implicit cleanup hide it.

`src/args.rs` remains the entry point for looking up the parameter structure. The file introduces `StructOpt` and sits directly alongside `crate::git`; this is enough to show that the parameters and Git-related paths need to be reviewed together. It does not establish the full relationship between template configuration and execution paths, so this proposal defines semantics only for the exposed choices, without treating the arrangement of implementation files as a conclusion.

An early draft separated three cases: the template requests initialization, the caller requests initialization, and the caller requests that initialization be disabled. That wording made the last case look like an exception, and reviewers could easily read it as "the template takes precedence unless handled otherwise." That wording has been discarded. Disabling initialization is not a corrective action; it is an explicit generation choice.

The decision is: when the caller does not pass --vcs, [template] vcs supplies the default for repository initialization; an explicit --vcs always takes precedence, and .git must not be created when the final choice is None.

This rule separates the sources into two layers. The template supplies only a default, allowing its usual environment to be recorded in configuration; caller parameters apply only to this generation run, allowing callers to use their own version control arrangements. When neither layer is present, retain the generator's existing default handling rather than introducing a third configuration source in this proposal.

None must hold true for the output directory, not merely mean that an initialization command is skipped. If the generation path writes Git metadata and then deletes it, hooks, error recovery, and directory checks may all observe that intermediate state; this is inconsistent with the caller's choice not to initialize. Implementation checks should therefore target the final directory and cover the combination where the template supplies a default but the caller explicitly disables initialization. Conversely, when the template makes no declaration and the caller explicitly selects initialization, that should use the same selection entry point rather than maintaining different creation logic for the two sources.

The withdrawal criteria are narrowed accordingly: if the implementation cannot guarantee the absence of `.git` when the final choice is None, do not merge the interface change described as "template defaults, caller Fang Ke overrides." Fix the timing of initialization first rather than silently downgrading the parameter to a suggestion. The template configuration wording must not continue to describe initialization as mandatory, since that could mislead callers.

The case-conversion helper proceeds alongside this decision but does not share its precedence logic. It is intended for name transformations in Rhai templates. The retained sample is `Hello HTTP World`, with `hello_http_world` as the result; the acronym HTTP is preserved as a single word in the result. This rule covers only this helper's word-splitting result; it does not extend to other normalization processes for project names, target directories, or Cargo crate names.

The implementation should not require template authors to piece together multiple case checks themselves. The Rhai entry point should make this one conversion rule stable, with templates simply consuming the result. This proposal does not need additional special conventions for converting ordinary words; samples containing consecutive uppercase letters already define the boundary of this change.

Two areas of work are not expanded by this decision. First, tag selection and template testing continue to be handled through their respective entry points, without tying them to VCS precedence. Second, whether template hooks can observe initialization state needs to be checked separately in the generation execution path; without evidence, do not make it part of the template contract.

Before merging, retain three categories of regression tests: the template supplies a default and the caller passes no parameter; the caller explicitly overrides the template; and the final choice is None. The first two verify source precedence, while the last verifies that the directory contains no leftover Git metadata. On the Rhai side, only the name sample containing an acronym needs to be retained, to prevent later changes from degrading `hello_http_world` into letter-by-letter splitting.

The old draft treated "disable initialization" as an exceptional branch still to be added; it is now a normal choice. The helper's scope remains unchanged.

# Project Identity and Template Revision Troubleshooting Tree

Start by looking at the generated directory name; do not immediately treat it as evidence of the template content. In the samples encountered recently, the init hook writes the project name back; other samples require content to be retrieved from a particular tag of a Git template. Both actions happen during generation, but the anomaly seen in the field may not come from the same place.

The working hypothesis is that the name obtained during the interactive phase is only the initial input. After the hook writes back a new name, the subsequent directory handling and Template Variables may need to be resolved again. This hypothesis is not yet tied to a specific call site; it can only be used to decide what to record first.

```text
Generated output is incorrect
├─ Did the hook write the project name?
│  ├─ Not sure
│  │  └─ Record the original input and actual directory first; do not attribute it to the hook
│  └─ Confirmed it did
│     ├─ Directory is still the original input
│     │  └─ Record the value written back and check whether subsequent steps picked it up
│     └─ Directory has changed
│        └─ Then check whether a project-name variable appears in the template
└─ Content looks like another template revision
   ├─ No recognizable template content
   │  └─ Do not decide whether the tag was selected incorrectly
   └─ Recognizable content is present
      └─ Record the selected tag and output separately
```

The old record checked only the target directory. This was useful because the directory was the first thing visible, but it left a gap: even if the directory name changed, the project name and crate name in the template might still use the initial input. Do not use "the directory has changed" as a substitute for checking the rendered result.

You can start by opening `src/template_variables/project_name.rs`. The file header directly depends on `heck::{ToKebabCase, ToSnakeCase}`, so the hyphenated and underscored forms provide adjacent clues about the conversion here. This does not show where the init hook runs, nor can import alone establish which value is the final source.

When retrieving a template by tag, first confirm whether the output contains anything that distinguishes the revision. If there is no such content, write only "Not yet compared"; do not guess which revision was selected based on the directory name, template address, or whether generation succeeded. Specifying a tag expresses an intent to select; it is not proof that the corresponding content was retrieved.

The old note's assessment was: once the hook changes the name and the directory follows suit, the project-name check can end. Retain this assessment provisionally; later, use a sample where the directory changed but the variable was not checked to decide whether it can still be used.

Next time in the field, record at minimum: the original project name, the value written by the hook, the actual directory, the form of the project name appearing in the template, and whether a tag was specified. If the template has no project-name variable, record that fact as observed as well; do not fill it in using the result of another generation.

# Project Identity and Template Revision Troubleshooting Tree

When generated results are abnormal, first split the notes into project identity and template revision. Previously, they were written as one continuous process, so during review it was easy to conclude "the directory is wrong, so the tag is wrong." This conclusion is not sufficiently supported: the directory is a generation target, while the template revision is source selection; either side may have a problem, or only one side may be missing observation data.

## Start from the old entry point, but do not treat the entry point as the cause

The earliest troubleshooting started from `src/template_variables/project_name.rs`. The file itself only provides clues around project-name format conversion; the file header shows:

```rust
use heck::{ToKebabCase, ToSnakeCase};
```

When you see a directory using hyphens and a crate using underscores, do not initially record the visual difference as a failure. The two forms may naturally be derived from the same project identity. What actually needs to be investigated is whether, after the hook renames it, the directory and rendered variables are still each taking their values from different sources.

The old rule was "A changed directory is enough." This rule is now marked **deprecated**, but do not delete it. It was the only result that could be observed reliably at the time; the problem is that it mistook a local observation for a complete judgment. A directory change can only show that path handling saw some new value; it cannot prove that Template Variables also left the interactive input at the same time.

## First preserve the identity sample completely

Do not start by generating repeatedly. The first time you see the hook rename something, write the following items in the same incident record:

- The project name entered during the interactive stage;
- The project name written by the init hook;
- The actual generated directory;
- The `project-name` visible after Template Rendering;
- The `crate_name` visible after Template Rendering.

If one item cannot be seen, do not infer it from another item. In particular, if you only see the directory and crate name, you cannot assert that `project-name` has been updated; the template may not have output it in this result. A blank is neither failure nor success; it only means that this sample provided no comparison point.

```text
Identity branch
│
├─ Unable to confirm that the hook wrote a name back
│  └─ First handle it as an ordinary generated result; do not record it as an identity-normalization anomaly
│
├─ The hook's write-back value is the same as the original input
│  └─ This is not a rename sample; retain the record but do not verify subsequent use after the rename
│
├─ The hook's write-back value differs, but the directory is still the original input
│  └─ Retain both values; check whether the write-back value is received by subsequent steps
│
├─ The hook's write-back value differs, the directory changes, but the variables still look like the original input
│  └─ Continue comparing the source of each variable; do not explain away the difference as format conversion
│
└─ The hook's write-back value differs, and the directory and all variables seen use the new identity
   └─ The identity branch ends for now; the template revision still needs to be checked separately
```

The phrase "variables still look like the original input" does not mean that the strings must be exactly identical. The directory, `project-name`, and `crate_name` may use different formats. What needs to be made explicit is which variable can still be traced to the original input and which variable already reflects the identity written back by the hook. `ToKebabCase` and `ToSnakeCase` can only help locate the objects being formatted; they cannot replace this comparison.

## A review that looked only at the directory

In one review, a changed directory was recorded as "recovered." In retrospect, that check did not read any project-name variable in the template; it only confirmed the path. It did not prove that the hook had not run, nor did it find a problem with tag selection; it only showed that the old rule had treated the directory as the stopping condition—correctly as a path observation, but too strongly as a conclusion.

After this review, the recording method was changed to write the original input first and then the value after the hook. If the two values are the same, the sample is not treated as a rename case; if they differ, only then are the directory and visible variables listed side by side. This prevents an ordinary generated result from being used in place of a counterexample involving a hook rename.

Keep manual records in the following format. Each field may be empty, but results from another generation run must not be mixed in.

```text
Original project name:
Hook write-back:
Actual directory:
project-name:
crate_name:
Location where the original input is still visible:
```

If the directory has changed and Template Variables has no viewable location, the record should stop at "Directory observed, variable not compared". Do not write "Project name fully synchronized". Conversely, if the template displays only one variable and the directory was not saved, write only "Variable observed, directory not compared".

## A separate sheet for template revision

When the template content looks like another version, first ask whether `--tag` was explicitly passed this time. The `generate`'s `--tag` is used to select the content corresponding to a specified tag in the Git template repository. It has no direct bearing on the judgment about the project-directory rename: a correct directory does not imply a correct selection, and a correct selection does not imply that the variables were updated after the hook.

A revision sample must retain at least two types of information: the selection value and content in the output that can actually distinguish the template version. Recording only the tag name is not enough; afterward, it will be impossible to distinguish between "the content was not fetched according to the selection" and "the output content cannot be compared at all".

```text
Template content does not look like the expected revision
│
├─ --tag not specified
│  └─ Do not attribute this to tag selection; leave this branch
│
├─ --tag specified, but the output has no content that can distinguish the revision
│  └─ Stop here; the current sample cannot compare the tag content
│
├─ --tag specified, the output distinguishes the revision, but the content does not match
│  └─ Retain the selection value and corresponding output; check the template source selection
│
└─ --tag specified, and the output content matches
   └─ The revision branch ends; do not use it to explain project-name variables
```

Here, "distinguishable" must come from template content that is actually visible after generation. A Git URL, generated directory, directory timestamp, or the default branch remembered by the observer cannot substitute for it. If the output cannot distinguish the revision, write "Cannot compare" in the record; do not guess a version just to close the branch.

Old guidance once treated "having a tag parameter" as evidence that the content had been fetched according to the tag. This practice should also be considered outdated. The option only says what the caller wants to select; the output content says whether this result conforms to that selection.

## Boundaries left by the review

The review confirmed that the two troubleshooting lines can end separately.

The project-identity side handles whether, after the value written back by the hook, the directory and Template Variables still use the value from the interactive stage. Here, you can trace back from `project_name.rs` to the adjacent formatting, but you cannot infer which implementation owns the hook from the file location.

The template-revision side handles whether, after the specified selection value, the final rendered content corresponds to the expected revision. Here, content that can distinguish versions must be retained; the directory name should not be used to infer it.

Therefore, while the identity branch has not ended, the revision branch may still have a definite result; even after the revision branch has ended, the identity variables may still be unchecked. If both branches are blank at the same time, retain the blanks separately; do not combine them into "template anomaly".

## Local locations still to investigate

- The relationship between the format conversion in `project_name.rs` and reading the value again after the hook still needs to be confirmed by following the actual references;
- The ordering between tag selection and determining the template root has not yet been fixed in this record;
- If the hook rename affects only the directory and not the rendered variables, retain the complete sample; do not explain it away with the difference between hyphens and underscores;
- If the output contains no content that can distinguish the revision, the revision branch can only stop in a not-compared state.

The old directory check remains above so that people entering through an old link can understand why only a path result was left before. The current troubleshooting starts with two records: one comparing project identity and one comparing template content.

The generated directory changed names, yet the template still showed the original input; that was the earliest symptom recorded on this page. Later, checks for fetching Git templates by tag also appeared in the same batch of generation records, so "wrong directory," "wrong variable," and "wrong template version" were at one point documented as the same type of anomaly. The old entry point usually led people to the directory name first, so this tree still starts with the directory; but do not let the directory stand in for the template content now.

First, separate the symptoms at hand. Until it is confirmed that the init hook wrote the project name, do not attribute the directory difference to identity normalization; until it is confirmed that the output contains template content that distinguishes revision, do not determine whether the tag was selected incorrectly. Both things can happen in one generation, but the result of one cannot be used to draw a conclusion about the other.

```text
Start: generated result does not match expectations
│
├─ Has it been confirmed that the init hook wrote the project name?
│  ├─ No or no record
│  │  └─ Do not enter the identity-normalization branch; retain only an ordinary directory or rendering symptom
│  └─ Yes
│     ├─ The directory is still the original input
│     │  └─ Record the original value and the written-back value; check whether subsequent steps receive the written-back value
│     ├─ The directory changed, but Template Variables still points to the original input
│     │  └─ Continue investigating identity recalculation; do not explain it as a formatting difference
│     └─ The directory and visible variable have both changed
│        └─ The identity branch can end
│
└─ Does the output contain content that distinguishes template revision?
   ├─ No
   │  └─ Do not determine whether the tag selection is correct
   └─ Yes
      ├─ --tag was not specified
      │  └─ Do not use the tag-anomaly branch
      ├─ The content does not match the specified tag
      │  └─ Record the selected value and the output; check the template source selection
      └─ The content matches the specified tag
         └─ The revision branch can end
```

This tree is not a call graph. It only specifies which value to collect first during the investigation and when to stop because the evidence is insufficient. The directory, Template Variables, and the template content are separate observables; one being correct must not cause the other two to be marked as correct.

## 2023-05-24: At First, Only the Directory Was Observed

The first record was brief: after the hook renamed the project, if the target directory changed accordingly, the project rename was considered successful. That conclusion was understandable at the time. The directory was the easiest object to find after generation, Template Variables did not appear consistently in every sample, and the template content selected by tag had not yet been included in the same record.

The original wording from the old notes is retained below:

> When the directory is correct, there is no need to check the project-name variable.
This statement **no longer applies**. It was once a time-saving sequence of checks, not a complete identity check. A correct directory only means that path handling used a new value, not that every subsequent variable in the template has stopped using the input from the interactive phase.

The original local navigation was `src/template_variables/project_name.rs`. The file header shows:

```rust
use heck::{ToKebabCase, ToSnakeCase};
```

This snippet made the directory form and the crate form look as though they were right next to each other. The difference between hyphens and underscores was therefore often misread as an anomaly, especially when the generated directory and Template Variables were compared at the same time. The old records did not distinguish between "different forms" and "different sources", so whenever something in one location looked like a reasonable kebab or snake form, it was easy to record that the project names were already consistent.

This early material supports only one reliable action: open the locations where project name formats are converted, and note the respective forms in which the directory and variables appear. You cannot infer where the init hook executes from the import, nor can you infer from this path's name that all subsequent variables are constructed here.

## Early working hypothesis, with no deletions or edits

The working hypothesis at the time was: the name obtained during the interactive phase is the default value, and the name written back by the hook mainly affects the target directory. Template Variables may continue to use the initial value, and as long as the rendered character form has no obvious errors, leave it alone for now.

This hypothesis was later withdrawn, but it is retained here because it explains why older troubleshooting records often contain only a directory name, a note that "the hook ran", and incomplete template output. It also explains why some people treated the difference in appearance between `project-name` and `crate_name` as the same problem.

The old hypothesis had two practical limitations.

First, it did not require saving the original input and the value written by the hook. Without these two reference points, an "old name" seen later might be a formatting result, or it might actually be the earlier input, with no way to distinguish the two.

Second, it did not require preserving the locations where the variables appeared in the template. The directory alone cannot tell you whether rendering used the same identity, or whether a particular variable was absent from the sample altogether.

Therefore, when starting from an old page or an old command record, do not fill in variable values that were not recorded at the time. If an old record lacks template output, acknowledge only that it can show a directory change; do not elevate it to evidence that the entire generation process was already consistently using the new name.

## 2024-04-22: Expand the identity sample to five values

The later review did not start by changing the implementation, but by changing the captured records into a side-by-side comparison. Whenever you confirm that the hook changed the name, first retain the following five items:

- The original project name from the interactive phase;
- The project name after the init hook writes it;
- The directory actually generated;
- The `project-name` that appears after rendering;
- The `crate_name` that appears after rendering.

These values do not need to be character-for-character identical. Directory names often need to retain the hyphenated form, while crate names often need the underscored form. When comparing them, ask whether they are still derived from the same identity, rather than forcing the two formats into exactly the same string.

For manual records, retain the blanks below. This allows some samples to have no visible variables; the blanks must be preserved, not filled in with results from another generation run.

```text
Original project name:
Value written by hook:
Actual directory:
project-name:
crate_name:
Locations where the original input is still visible:
```

If the value written by the hook is the same as the original input, this record does not constitute a renaming case. It can show that the hook path was exercised, but cannot be used to verify normalization after a rename. Only when the two values differ do the directory and variables have a shared baseline for comparison.

If only the directory and crate name were saved, the record should say "Directory and crate name observed, project-name not compared". If the template only displays `project-name`, do not assume that `crate_name` has also been synchronized. One fewer variable in the template output does not indicate an error; it simply means that no place to observe that variable was provided in this run.

## 2024-04-23: Supplementary review notes

The review pointed out that the original linear write-up treated format conversion as source identification. `ToKebabCase` and `ToSnakeCase` show that the two conversions occur around the project name, but do not prove that variables at every location read the same input.

The assessment after the supplementary note is narrower: correct formatting cannot compensate for inconsistent sources. If the directory already uses the post-hook value, but a variable can still be traced back to the original interactive input, the identity branch remains unresolved; conversely, if a variable looks like it is in the old format, its format alone is not enough to conclude that it still comes from the old input, and the original value and the written-back value are still needed as references.

At the time, an easily overlooked stopping condition was also retained: when either the original input or the value written by the hook is missing, do not classify "inconsistent names" as a post-hook identity issue. You can continue recording the directory and rendered text, but the conclusion should stop at "identity source unconfirmed". This is closer to the actual evidence than attributing every name difference to `project_name.rs`.

The review did not include tag selection in this five-item table. The reason is simple: the tag determines the Git template's revision, while project identity determines the subsequent use of paths and variables after generation. Both lines of investigation may need to be checked at the same time, but the required outputs are different.

## A failed directory recheck

One recheck examined only the generated directory. The directory already used the form visible after the hook wrote its value, so the record was marked "restored". Looking back, this check did not read any project-name variables in the template, nor did it save the original input and the value written by the hook side by side.

This attempt did not prove that there was a problem with the tag branch, nor did it prove that the hook had not run. It only invalidated the old stopping criterion: a directory change is not enough.

The failure was not in the directory check itself. The directory should still be recorded, because it is one result in the identity chain. The failure was in allowing one result to override the others. The revised approach is not to skip the directory, but to place it alongside the two variables, allowing any one item to temporarily have no observed value.

This review also left us with an edge case: even if `project-name` and `crate_name` both have formats that "look correct", they may not come from the same source. One value may already reflect the hook's write-back, while the other still retains the interactive input, with both merely happening to conform to their respective format rules. For samples like this, you cannot write "the name looks fine", and must record the value still visible in each location.

## The deprecated shortcut

The old approach had two steps: first check whether the directory had been renamed; after it was renamed, check whether generation succeeded. If both were true, Template Variables and the template contents were no longer checked.

This method did save effort when the directory was easy to check and the template contents were hard to identify, but it should now be used only as an initial observation. It is not suitable as a stopping criterion, for the following reasons:

1. A directory change cannot replace a comparison of `project-name` and `crate_name`;
2. Successful generation cannot replace a comparison of the Git template revision;
3. Passing a selection option does not establish that the output content already matches the selected value;
4. Plausible variable formats do not establish that the variables' sources are already consistent.

The old steps are not being deleted so that people arriving from old links can understand why some records include only the directory, or only "tag has been passed". These historical samples can still be used to locate a starting point, but cannot be used directly to end the current investigation.

## Another track for template content

`generate` supports using `--tag` to select the content corresponding to a specified tag in a Git template repository. A common misreading must be avoided here: the project directory name cannot prove which revision was selected. The directory is part of the target project, not a version marker for the template content.

The revision branch only needs to answer two questions: whether `--tag` was explicitly specified for this run, and whether the generated output contains content sufficient to distinguish the template revision. If either answer is missing, do not describe "looks like the old template" as a selection failure.

```text
Unexpected template content
│
├─ --tag not explicitly specified
│  └─ Do not attribute this to tag selection; preserve the observation, exit this branch
│
├─ --tag specified, but the output has no content that distinguishes revisions
│  └─ Stop: the current sample does not allow a comparison of tag content
│
├─ --tag specified, the output distinguishes revisions, but the content does not match
│  └─ Save the specified value and its corresponding output, check template source selection
│
└─ --tag specified, the output content matches
   └─ The revision branch ends; do not use it to explain identity variables
```

"Content that distinguishes revisions" must be template content actually visible after generation. Git addresses, directory timestamps, whether generation succeeded, the default branch as remembered by the observer, none of these are comparison material for this branch. When the output does not distinguish revisions, you can accurately write "cannot compare"; this is not a request to modify the template further, but a statement that the current sample is insufficient to determine whether the selection was correct.

According to the old instructions, supplying the tag parameter was enough to interpret subsequent content according to that tag. This statement is also marked as **deprecated**. The parameter indicates the intended selection, while the output content is what shows whether the result of this run matches that intent. Record both together, so that source selection and rendering anomalies are not later conflated into a single judgment.

## A parallel record, not a sequential checklist

Identity samples and revision samples should be kept separately. The former records how the identity is used before and after the hook, while the latter records the selected value and template content. The purpose is not to make the table more complete, but to prevent the result of one branch from overriding the other branch.

Identity sample:

```text
Whether init hook renaming has been confirmed:
Original input:
What the hook wrote:
Directory:
project-name:
crate_name:
Where the original input is still visible:
```

revision sample:

```text
Whether --tag was used:
Specified tag:
Content in the output that distinguishes revisions:
Whether that content matches the specified value:
Identity branch status:
```

The last line only reminds later readers not to merge the two samples. It is not intended to put identity results into the revision conclusion. For example, even when the directory and variables already match, the template content may still be impossible to identify; even when the output content already matches the selected value, the post-hook variables may still not have been checked.

If there is insufficient evidence on one side, stop that side of the investigation. Do not fill in the hook-renaming sample with variables obtained during a normal generation run, and do not use a directory from another generation run to establish what content corresponds to this run's tag. Both ways of filling in gaps will leave subsequent review without a shared baseline of the observed state.

## The distinction retained from the old meeting excerpts

One brief distinction was retained in subsequent discussions: project identity and template revision do not follow the same decision tree.

The project identity side asks whether, after the init hook writes the name, the target directory and Template Variables still use the fallback values from the interactive stage. `src/template_variables/project_name.rs` is the local reference point for checking format conversions; the `ToKebabCase` and `ToSnakeCase` within it can help locate different representations of the project name, but cannot replace verification of the actual references.

The template revision side asks whether, after a selection value is specified, the template content ultimately rendered corresponds to that revision. This is not automatically established by a change in the directory name, nor is it automatically established by a particular Template Variables already being correct.

This boundary only constrains how troubleshooting records are written, and does not assign ownership of the implementation. For cases with anomalies on both sides, it is best to save the observations from both sides together; if one side lacks evidence, leave only that side unknown, rather than filling in a conclusion using the other side's results.

## Two remaining sticking points

The first point is where the value written back by the hook enters the subsequent workflow. `project_name.rs` provides nearby context for project name conversion, but this page does not identify it as the hook's implementation location. When checking back, first examine the formatting object here, then follow the actual references to confirm whether the written-back value enters directory processing and variable construction.

The second point is the relationship between the template root and tag selection. This page only requires comparing the selected revision using the output content, and does not prescribe their internal order. If the output has no distinguishing content, the revision branch remains without a comparison; do not assume that the template root has already been determined in a particular order just to complete the flowchart.

These two unknowns cannot be combined. The former lacks the point in the identity chain where the value is obtained, while the latter lacks material for comparing template content. They will appear in the same review, but each requires a different next observation.

## 2025-07-18: Current criteria

The old rules, review addenda, and failure reviews above have been retained to explain why the current checks no longer look only at the directory. After confirming that this is an init hook rename case, apply the following requirements:

> The init hook may first write the original project-name; the target directory must then be normalized to project-bar, and project-name and crate_name must be recalculated based on it, rather than continuing to use the interactive fallback name.

This requirement concerns only project identity. It does not specify which revision to select for a Git template, nor can the fact that the tag branch has already passed substitute for checking the variables. The directory, `project-name` and `crate_name` may each use an appropriate format; the requirement here is that they no longer use the interactive fallback name after the hook performs a rename.

When verifying the case at hand, first obtain the original input and the value written by the hook. Then compare the actual directory with the visible variables. If the directory has changed but the original input is still visible in one or both variables, the identity branch remains open. If the directory and both visible variables are derived from the post-hook identity, the identity branch can be closed, even if the revision branch still requires a separate comparison. If the hook did not perform a rename, this requirement draws no conclusion about the normal generation path.

As before, start the trace-back adjacent to the format conversion for `src/template_variables/project_name.rs`, then follow the actual references to confirm where the written-back value enters the subsequent flow. Do not treat `heck::{ToKebabCase, ToSnakeCase}` as evidence for the entire generation flow; it can only narrow down where to inspect the project-name representation.

## Legacy appendix: The former two-step quick check

The following two steps are still retained for people arriving via old links. They are not the current completion criteria.

1. Check whether the generated directory has been renamed; if it has, assume that the post-hook flow has fully switched to the new name.
2. After specifying a tag, check whether generation succeeds; if it does, assume that the output comes from that tag.

The first step was invalidated by a follow-up check in which "the directory changed, but the variables were not compared". The second step is also insufficient to show that the output contents correspond to the selected revision. They can serve as a starting point for initial observations, but cannot replace the five identity records and the template-content comparison.

The legacy appendix has not been removed because some historical cases left only a directory name and a note saying "tag was passed in". When working with these records, first acknowledge their limits: a directory change cannot account for the variables, and the presence of an option cannot account for the template contents. Once you have filled in enough information from the same case to make the comparisons, complete the identity and revision branches separately.

## Issues not yet split out

After the template source is selected by tag, determining the template root and checking project identity sometimes come up in the same review. This page does not group the two together as a "template issue". If the revision cannot be identified from the output, keep the template contents marked as not compared; if the value written by the hook was not retained, keep the identity source marked as unconfirmed. Both stopping conditions can exist at the same time.

# Rhai system command authorization experiment notes

The command runs in the staging template directory copied into the generated project afterward, not in the final project directory itself.

This round, start by bringing the hook-related checks back to `tests/integration/hooks.rs`. The dependencies at the top of the file already show that these aren't notes on running a script in isolation: `indoc` is used to preserve template snippets, `OutputAssertExt` and `PredicateStrExt` are reserved for command output assertions, and `binary` and `tmp_dir` prepare the project directory.

Two issues are mixed together in this round. The first is the authorization boundary for system commands in Rhai; the second is how nested conditions behave when they receive boolean values. They share the hook test entry point, but don't treat the result of a command authorization test as evidence that conditional rendering is covered. The conditions portion remains just a counterexample to be added in the same directory; next time, write out separately what content remains when the inner condition receives true and when it receives false.

Template hooks should only reach system commands after authorization; the unauthorized path should stop before command execution. The constraint here is that a Rhai hook can call system::command(program, arguments) only when the caller explicitly passes --allow-commands. The command runs in the staging template directory that is copied into the generated project afterward, not in the final project directory itself, and execution failure must abort generation.

So when checking, distinguish "Template Rendering complete" from "hook succeeded." The former only shows that the project directory and template contents are in place; it cannot vouch for the latter. If the latter fails, generation must not continue and return a success status. The existing output assertion tools are sufficient for both observations; these checks won't be split out into another set of helpers yet.

For the additional nested-condition test, change only one variable: keep the template and generation directory the same, and set the inner input to boolean true, then false. Check whether the conditional branch is selected by value, rather than the test passing by chance because the boolean is treated as a string. If this additional test exposes a failure unrelated to command authorization, record it under conditions, not as an exception to the authorization rules.

# Configuration File and Working Directory Decision Record

This record initially tied two observations too closely together: the path taken when the default configuration file is absent, and the directory the caller remains in after a library call finishes. Both were placed under 0.14 Compatibility Train, and early code reading for both began around the generation entry point, so the initial draft used "generation completed normally" as their shared working terminology. That wording was convenient, but it conflated subjects that needed to be verified separately.

The initial draft did not classify them as the same implementation defect. The decision at the time was simply to reject an easier acceptance approach: the fact that generation has finished does not establish that configuration reading and the caller's directory state are both correct. Configuration reading concerns which branch is taken when input is missing; directory restoration concerns whether a library call preserves the process's original current location. Both issues can occur together, or only one can occur.

There were two options at the time.

- Write "Quiet Path for Default Configuration File" and "Working Directory Restoration After Library Call" as one broad regression check, retaining only one result.
- Separate the two: on the configuration side, follow the discovery entry point to find matching paths; on the directory side, retain the states before and after the call, then determine whether there is a common cause.

The first approach is not merely about making the document a little shorter; its cost is a result that is difficult to interpret. If generation completes, readers still do not know whether it skipped a configuration branch or whether the caller's current directory changed. If the directory changes, that also does not directly imply that configuration loading failed. The initial draft chose the second option, retaining two entry points and two unresolved items; that choice remains valid.

## Reading Starting Points Retained from the Initial Draft

The starting point on the configuration side was `src/app_config.rs`. This was not because the filename itself could provide a conclusion, but because the earlier investigation notes used terms such as configuration, loading, and file to lead the reading here. At the top of the file, we can see:

```rust
use anyhow::{Context, Result};
use console::style;
use serde::Deserialize;
use std::{
```

These lines do not tell us what the final return result will be for an absent default configuration file, nor do they list configuration filenames or the search order. They only constrain the early assessment to a very narrow scope: the configuration module deals with at least error context, display styling, and deserialization, so the missing-default-file path cannot be handled merely with the four-character label "read failure". It was reasonable for the initial draft to stop here; there was not enough material at the time to turn the quiet path into a concrete implementation commitment.

The directory side had no equivalent source-code anchor. Initially, some were inclined to keep looking near the configuration module, because the location used for reading might change during generation. That association was later retained as an old hypothesis, not as a basis for the decision. The caller's current working directory is part of the state after the library call completes; even if configuration reading takes place in a particular directory, that does not establish whether the directory was or was not restored when the call ended.

Therefore, the initial draft's statement that "both observations are near the generation entry point" was only a habit for locating the issue, not a causal judgment. Subsequent reading no longer requires them to fall within the same function, file, or portion of the lifecycle. This old assessment is retained in the record to show that the later separation was not an ad hoc change of topic, but a narrowing of the original classification.

## Adjustments After the Cards Were Introduced

CG-206 later became the navigation entry point for the configuration side. It requires following the discovery process for "Quiet Path for Default Configuration File" from the repository root and retaining the final list of matches. The emphasis here is on starting from the repository root, rather than first assuming that a particular configuration object must be responsible for all the behavior. For this card, the current decision is to continue organizing the material around the actual matching paths; until a list of matches is available, do not extrapolate from the imports or filename of `src/app_config.rs` into a complete set of rules for the default configuration file.

This also corrects an ambiguous statement in the initial draft. The draft treated "quiet" as an outcome already ready for direct acceptance testing. The available material does not provide the default configuration file's name, search locations, priority, or the full output shown when handling a default file. The historical term "quiet path" is now retained to identify the subject of the investigation; by itself, it no longer represents a specific hard-coded error message or one unique return behavior.

CG-223 brings the other track back to the state after the library call. A counterexample was added to that card in subsequent records, and the card moved from to-do to in progress. The specific content of the counterexample is not included on this page and cannot replace the original comparison of directory states; however, it is sufficient to refute the simplified judgment that "if the lifecycle appears complete, there is no need to check the current directory again".

The later addendum likewise confirmed only the Generation Lifecycle portion. One aspect of Working Directory Restoration After Library Call remains unconfirmed, with the input and output retained in a temporary repository state snapshot. This boundary matters: what has been confirmed is a particular portion of Generation Lifecycle, not the conclusion that the caller's directory has been restored. Previously, listing the two together as "compatibility after generation completes" could give the impression that the directory issue had also been closed out; they are now explicitly kept separate.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> ConfigDiscovery
    ConfigDiscovery: Default configuration file discovery
    ConfigDiscovery --> ConfigHits: Final list of matches still to be added
    [*] --> CallerBefore
    CallerBefore: Directory state before the library call
    CallerBefore --> CallerAfter: Directory state after the library call still to be checked
```

The two state tracks in the diagram show only the verification sequence in the current record. The configuration track runs from the discovery entry point to the final list of matches; the directory track runs from the state before the call to the state after it. They have no merge node here because the available material has not yet linked them to a common cause.

## Judgments Not Adopted This Time

During review, we reconsidered the approach of "downgrading the directory issue to residual test-environment state". Its appeal was that part of the generation process itself had already been confirmed, while the temporary repository could make directory observations look like environmental differences. However, adopting this judgment would first require proving that the library call did not change the directory between the before-call and after-call states; that is precisely the point that remains unconfirmed in the existing record. The issue was therefore not classified as residual environmental state.

Nor did we make the reverse judgment that the default configuration file's path caused the directory change. The configuration path and current directory may be related within the same call, but no material on this page links them in a one-way causal relationship. If they are later found to be triggered by the same directory-switching operation, new evidence should be added before merging them; "both involve paths" cannot replace that evidence.

Another rejected formulation was to label the configuration module directly as responsible for directory restoration. `src/app_config.rs` remains on this page because it is a readable entry point for the configuration issue; it does not automatically explain the state at the end of the library call. The compatibility cost of this approach is small: investigation requires following one additional entry point, but an unconfirmed process state will not be attributed to the wrong module.

## Current Decision

This page keeps these two requirements in 0.14 Compatibility Train as parallel records, rather than conditions that prove one another.

1. Quiet Path for Default Configuration File, to be checked through the configuration discovery process. CG-206 is the navigation entry point for this track, and the final list of matches should determine where subsequent changes or regression checks belong.
2. Working Directory Restoration After Library Call, to be checked against the states before and after the call. The temporary repository state snapshot in CG-223 retains this track's input and output; confirmation of Generation Lifecycle cannot replace this step.
3. While neither track has new direct evidence, do not elevate "generation succeeded", "the configuration module is readable", or "the lifecycle has been confirmed" into a conclusion that the other track is complete.

Keeping them parallel does not require the two to use the same set of tests, nor does it require them to share the same code ownership. It only constrains the order of judgment: first clarify configuration discovery and the caller's directory state separately, then discuss whether they need to be handled together. This avoids a regression check leaving only an "everything is normal" conclusion without being able to answer which state was actually observed.

## Corrections to the Earlier Wording

The initial draft's wording "generation completed normally" is no longer used as a basis for judgment. It is retained because it reflects the working hypothesis at the time; however, it can now describe only a broad observation, not prove how an absent default configuration file is handled or that the caller's directory remains unchanged after the library call returns.

The initial draft also made `src/app_config.rs` sound too much like the overall entry point. More accurately: it is a local module already identified in the configuration investigation. The dependencies at the top of the file can help guide further reading of adjacent material related to error context, display, and deserialization, but should not be treated as a map of the entire generation process. Verification of directory restoration should still begin with state changes across the library call, rather than reasoning backward from this file's name.

DOC-16 document the interface review of no-VCS and paths containing spaces. That review also involves paths, but it is not included in the basis for this decision. The concerns here are the discovery path for the default configuration and the caller's current directory when the library call ends; whether interface arguments are passed natively and whether VCS is initialized remain within their respective review scopes.

## Observed Evidence Still to Be Added

What still needs to be added on the configuration side is the final list of matches required by CG-206. Once the list is available, the matching locations and excluded paths should be appended directly to this decision, rather than summarized again as "configuration loading has been checked". If the matches show that the default file never passed through `src/app_config.rs`, retain a record of this early error in locating the issue and move the reading starting point to the actual branch.

What still needs to be added on the directory side is a repeatable before-and-after comparison of a call, which must correspond to the state snapshot in CG-223. The current addendum already states that this part still contains unconfirmed items, so this record does not preemptively state that restoration succeeded, that the directory was not restored, or which layer changed the directory. What should be added to this record is the state difference itself and where it occurs, not speculation about the temporary repository environment.

The two tracks may ultimately be presented in the same regression run, but their presentation order will no longer be determined by "whether generation completed". First list the locations actually traversed during configuration discovery, then list the directory states before and after the library call; only when both sets of records are present should their possible common cause be discussed.
