# no-VCS and the spaces-in-path approach

This round of interface review will first take up two issues that are easy to conflate: after selecting no-VCS, which repository-related actions remain in the generation process; and when the target path contains spaces, whether the path remains a single value from parameter parsing through directory creation. The former cannot be judged only by whether a directory was ultimately initialized, and the latter cannot be judged only by a log line that looks correct.

There are tentatively two ways to handle no-VCS. The first is to skip initialization at the end of the flow; it requires fewer changes and is closer to how the existing entry point is understood. The downside is that source preparation, temporary-directory handling, or template-side decisions earlier in the flow may still run as though a repository exists. The second is to pass the selection downstream when the generated configuration is formed, so later steps can use it to decide whether repository context is needed. The second approach touches more call sites, but its boundary is easier to define.

The path issue should not be solved by concatenating the parameters into a single command string. Spaces are not invalid characters; splitting should happen as late as possible. The trial implementation should pass the target path as a path object and hand it to that interface only where an external action actually needs to be started; the intermediate layer should not add quoting.

The interface options are currently concentrated around `src/args.rs`. This is where `StructOpt`, error returns, and `crate::git` are directly adjacent. Start by confirming where the selection value lands from this entry point, then decide which generation steps need to be touched.

The recommendation is to first run a narrow trial of the second no-VCS approach and prepare a target directory containing spaces as an observation item in the same round. Still undecided: whether the template source itself needs to distinguish between the two modes; and whether existing callers' handling of the path parameter has already split the string. If the trial forces changes to the source selector, first revert to an approach that adjusts only the generation-target side.

# Proposal for no-VCS and Paths with Spaces

At the time of the old draft, the discussion focused on whether "disabling version control" and "paths containing spaces" would affect each other at the same entry point. In retrospect, that grouping went a bit too far: the two share generation parameters, but their failure points differ. no-VCS concerns whether the generation stage gets repository context; paths containing spaces concern whether argument values are reinterpreted at handoff. Keeping them on one page was meant to prevent conflicting descriptions of the same interface change, not to imply that a single change must resolve both.

The old proposal is retained below. At the time, the preference was to treat no-VCS as an initialization switch at the end of the workflow: prepare the template and target as usual, then skip creating a repository at the end. The appeal was that the change looked narrowly scoped and was easy to align with the help text. The gap is that "not initialized" does not tell us whether repository-related decisions have already been made upstream. If the caller sees a project whose directory has not been initialized, but an intermediate step still treats it as having a repository, the choice shown in the interface does not match the actual boundary.

Another candidate approach is to pass the VCS choice down with the generation configuration. That way, each step requiring repository context can use the same value to decide whether to run. The cost is that each step's role needs to be checked individually: some only prepare the template source, some initialize the output project, and some may only touch Git-adjacent areas during error handling or cleanup. The old draft grouped all of these as "Git steps," a classification too broad to use directly to set the scope of changes.

`src/args.rs` is still the first place to look. The visible nearby elements include `StructOpt`, error returns from `anyhow`, and `crate::git`; this is a useful place to confirm where the command-line choice originates, but not to determine, on its own, where responsibility for the downstream generation flow lies. During the trial, first trace the choice value from the argument entry point to the generation configuration, then list the nodes that actually read it. Pushing all behavior into the argument layer just because `crate::git` appears in the file would conflate responsibility for paths with responsibility for source selection.

The old conclusion for paths still stands: do not format the target path into a piece of text for downstream code to split again. A directory name containing spaces is a single path value. Callers should not be required to add quotes themselves, nor should an intermediate layer guess whether quotes are already present. The candidate implementation is to retain a path object or an equivalent native representation after argument parsing, until the point where the target directory is created, the working directory is changed, or the value is handed to an external interface. What needs checking is not "whether the string contains spaces," but whether each handoff turns one value into multiple arguments.

However, there was an imprecise inference here: if the target directory could be created, that was taken to mean the path was being passed in its native form. That criterion is no longer used. Directory creation usually covers only local path usage and is no substitute for checking later handoffs; conversely, retaining a native value at one point does not establish that no caller has already concatenated it into a string upstream. The old draft's "one directory with spaces is enough to prove it" should be treated only as a minimal sample, not a conclusion.

The recommendation is to keep the trial scope very narrow:

- Choose a local path sample that requires no changes to the template content and has spaces in the generated target directory's name;
- Exercise the default version-control choice and the no-VCS choice separately, recording the resulting directory layout and whether any additional repository actions occur;
- Inspect the path value's representation at the argument entry point, in the generation configuration, and at the actual handoff points; do not add quotes to the path;
- If the template source selector needs to change, stop expanding this trial and first discuss source selection and output project initialization as separate concerns.

This does not require every intermediate action to be identical across the two paths. The default choice may need initialization, while the point of no-VCS is that skipping one action at the end should not pass for complete isolation. In the comparison, look only at differences directly related to this choice: whether the output project is treated as needing a repository, and whether the path value ceases to be a single value at any boundary.

The later card CG-207 designated no-VCS Full Boundaries as the entry point for post-upgrade regression checks, requiring it to be run as shown in the help text and then checking what the user could still see. CG-224 called for finding the two current documents with conflicting claims about passing paths containing spaces in their native form, and confirming the maintenance page and the owner responsible for updates. These two cards can help locate later material, but they cannot substitute for making the design choices left open here: they describe what needs to be checked and have not selected an implementation for this old proposal.

The tentative order for the candidate approaches remains: first establish an explicit place for the VCS choice in the generation configuration, then confirm which steps read it; for paths, start by eliminating string concatenation in the intermediate layer. If the former expands into template source parsing, or the latter requires changing the shape of arguments passed by existing callers, withdraw this combined trial and create separate changes. This would be slower, but would avoid rewriting source logic along the way just to prove no-VCS.

Three questions remain open. First, is template source preparation within the scope of no-VCS, or is that scope limited to the output project? Second, do all target paths passed by existing callers come from the same argument wrapper? Third, are there branches on error paths that read repository state only during cleanup? The old draft did not answer these questions. They are retained here to prevent later maintenance work from misreading "no `.git`" as meaning that all behavior has already been isolated.

# Git Author Identity and test Mode Decision Record

This page was not originally intended to document a complete generation chain. 0.14 Compatibility Train placed "Git Config Author Identity Fallback" and "Template Expansion Test Mode" in the same batch of work, and early readers could easily interpret the adjacent names as a sequence. The record was retained because people might look for old clues through the author-variable filename; but its decision scope has always been narrower than that of a command guide.

The first draft in May addressed a documentation question first: whether to combine the two items into one narrative. The combined account flowed smoothly, starting with author variables, moving on to Liquid expansion, and placing test mode last as verification. However, no output was retained at the time to prove that these steps occurred in sequence. Nor was there a sample showing which author value the test saw. Adopting this account directly would lead readers to interpret "requirements in the same batch" as "the same call path".

The alternative was to document them side by side on the same page. Author fallback would retain only the entry point and discussion scope on the variable side, while test mode would retain only the item name on the expansion side. This sacrificed a continuous reading sequence without inventing causality to fill in missing execution records. So the side-by-side approach on the same page was chosen at the time. That choice remains the actual decision preserved on this page: it was not intended to determine which source must take precedence, nor to prove that test mode already covered author identity.

## The Entry Point Preserved from the Old Draft

Early drafts treated `src/template_variables/authors.rs` as the starting point for the author identity issue. The currently visible file header is:

```rust
use anyhow::Result;
use git2::{Config as GitConfig, Repository as GitRepository};
use std::env;
```

`GitConfig`, `GitRepository` and `env` appear in the same file header, which is enough to establish the file as an entry point for investigating local relationships among author variables. This alone cannot establish the read order, nor can it establish what happens when a source is missing. One passage in the old draft overstated the case, effectively equating the file entry point with the fallback rules themselves; the trace of that historical judgment is preserved here, but it is now treated only as a starting point for investigation.

At the time, the three declarations were not arranged into a fixed chain such as "repository before configuration" or "environment before configuration". Adjacency among declarations is not the same as the order in which values are obtained at runtime. Listing them in order would add a decision to the page where no function-level material was available. The May page also contained no reusable sample of a concrete author identity result, so the first draft stopped at the entry point and scope.

This is also why author fallback was not written up as command-line parameter documentation. The available material places it in the Template Variables context of `src/template_variables/authors.rs`. The generation stage that calls it, the handling of default values and the final form passed to Liquid cannot be inferred from the file header. The old draft did not contain these details, and later versions did not fill the gaps with a generalized workflow.

## Two Candidate Decisions

The review at the time actually compared ways of organizing the page, not implementation approaches.

**Combined record.** This approach places author identity, template expansion and test mode together in the order a reader might perform the operations. The benefit is fewer entry points, allowing readers to continue along one thread. The cost is that it silently introduces several assumptions that were not preserved in the record: author identity is always read before expansion testing; test mode always observes the author variables; test results can in turn prove that fallback occurred. None of these three assumptions was supported by output from that time.

**Side-by-side records.** This approach treats author identity as one local issue thread and test mode as a separate expansion thread. Readers need to identify which subject they want to investigate first, and the page does not manufacture a call relationship merely through adjacent headings. The cost is that there is no smooth overall workflow connecting the two requirements, and source code or execution material must be consulted separately afterward.

Side-by-side records were chosen. The compatibility cost was accepted: one page cannot provide complete answers for both author identity and test mode. Preserving this limitation is more important than turning the page into an apparently coherent but unsupported entry point. The relevant specific functions, command output and failure samples were not included in this decision record at the time.

## The Author Identity Side

The old version's working hypothesis was: finding Git-related declarations in the author-variable file would allow the author identity fallback path to be reconstructed further. This claim was later narrowed. The filename and the three `use` declarations can help locate the subject, but they are neither call relationships nor rules governing how configuration, repository and environment values override one another.

So the author thread actually preserved on this page contains only three things: the starting point for investigation is `src/template_variables/authors.rs`; the file header directly contains `GitConfig`, `GitRepository` and `env`; the detailed precedence for author identity fallback was not settled on this page. The two later versions did not turn "not settled" into a new design conclusion, but instead retained the boundaries of the old decision.

Some people called this thread the overall entry point for the compatibility train. That name still appears in old references, but its scope is too broad. At most, it indicates where to begin checking material on the Template Variables side. It did not bring all template sources, generation destination directories or expansion actions into this page, nor did it turn neighboring items into responsibilities of the same module.

## The test Mode Side

"Template Expansion Test Mode" appeared in the first draft only as an expansion-side item awaiting verification. Details that were not preserved include: what test command was configured, how subsequent arguments were passed in, at what point in expansion the test occurred, and what kind of result the page should record on failure. Its appearance in the same batch as author fallback cannot fill these gaps.

The abandoned phrasing was "use test mode to verify author fallback". This phrasing looked convenient, but it actually fixed the test's observation target, execution order and interpretation of results all at once. Even if someone later reviewed the old test mode description, that review alone could not produce a missing execution output. So test mode remained on its own item thread and was not treated as evidence of author fallback.

Side-by-side documentation also does not mean the two threads can never intersect. It only means this page lacks enough material to connect them. If a concrete sample later appears that contains both author-variable results and test execution results, the relationship should be reassessed using that sample, rather than inferring implementation isolation from this page's side-by-side decision. This limitation describes the documentation approach at the time, not a prediction about future implementation.

## Changes Left After Review

CG-211 later had two status changes: it moved from To Do to In Progress on 2025-10-21, and from In Progress to Done on 2025-10-22. This added a dated trace of progress and completion for "Git Config Author Identity Fallback", but came with no author value, read order or Template Variables output. It is therefore treated here only as a follow-up record on the author thread, without recasting card status as an implementation conclusion.

CG-228 left `docs_reviewed` on 2025-10-30. This shows that the old description of "Template Expansion Test Mode" was read. It is not output from a test command, nor is it a success or failure result. The review action changed the page's recorded history, but did not change the side-by-side boundary chosen in May.

These two later traces belong to the two threads separately. CG-211 gave author fallback a follow-up progress record; CG-228 gave test mode a documentation review record. There is no sample run covering both, so there is no reason to rewrite the two items as a single generation sequence in v2.

## Scope Expansions Not Adopted During Review

A broader idea for the page also came up during review: turning it into an overview of author variables, expansion execution and compatibility testing for 0.14. This could reduce navigation, but would also pull in command entry points, test arguments and failure handling that had not been preserved. This idea was not adopted.

The file header of `src/template_variables/authors.rs` was not treated as an interface contract either. `anyhow::Result` can only serve as a record of an error-type dependency visible in the file, not as a basis for stating specific error messages on this page. `GitConfig` and `GitRepository` can only establish adjacency among local objects, not provide the configuration read order in place of the function bodies. The presence of `env` also cannot, on its own, determine whether environment variables override other sources.

Expanding these declarations into complete rules would make the page appear more certain than the actual material warrants. # Parent Directory and pre hook Plan

This review keeps two easily conflated issues separate: the generation target is determined using an explicitly provided parent directory, while the state produced by the pre hook still needs to be carried into Liquid expansion. Both lie between the entry point and rendering, but what they pass along is different. The former is the path and discovery result, while the latter is state the template can read; they should not be merged into a vague "context".

## Trade-offs

`--destination` is limited to the parent directory containing the generated project. After the entry point receives this parameter, it retains the relative path supplied by the user and the status returned by the tool, then passes the determined target location to the subsequent generation stage. This means local path templates do not have to infer the location again from the current working directory, and the caller can see before expansion whether path resolution succeeded.

There are two candidate points in the flow. Option A normalizes the relative path at the entry point, and subsequent stages consume only the normalized result; Option B retains the original relative path and normalizes it after the target directory is determined. A centralizes path handling and makes error locations visible earlier, but it changes the shape of the path that a subsequent hook might see. B is closer to the existing discovery flow, but makes the caller and hook interpret the same input differently. The recommendation at this point is to try A first, retain the original value for error display, and not use the current working directory as an implicit additional source. The normalization timing still needs to be confirmed against the code path.

The pre hook should not pass the entire internal return object straight into Liquid. The recommendation is to establish a clear state-passing chain, include only the state the template already needs, and assemble it before expansion begins. This keeps the hook's side effects from becoming the sole source of Template Variables, and keeps the field shape locally controllable during later changes. No final decision is made yet on the representation of empty state, whether expansion should continue after a hook failure, or field naming; these items should be determined by the implementation path and caller results.

## Verification Entry Point and Rollback Conditions

From `src/interactive.rs`, inspect the code adjacent to the entry point. The file header shows `use crate::{`, `use anyhow::Result;`, `use console::style;`, and `use dialoguer::theme::ColorfulTheme;`; these declarations are enough to locate the local inspection starting point, but not enough to infer the final return value. The check should separately record the parent directory's relative path, target location, and status returned by the tool, then confirm whether the pre hook's state actually reaches Liquid. Post-Hook Timing After Expansion remains in DOC-22; it is not merged here.

Validation should first cover one local path template: explicitly pass a parent directory, check path retention and target location; then have the pre hook change one state value and check the value read during expansion. If the entry point cannot reliably retain parent-directory information, roll back to the old entry point; do not let later stages guess the path again. If the state fields cannot be determined reliably from the code path, first disable Liquid exposure, retaining only the parent-directory propagation that has already been confirmed. Until caller results and failure branches are covered, this remains a provisional proposal.

# post hook and default branch troubleshooting tree

First, check two symptoms in the generation process: template files have already appeared in the target directory, but the post hook output looks as if it never happened; or, when using a local template, the result doesn't match the expected default-branch content. Investigate the two separately first; don't combine the attribution just because both occur near the end of generation.

If expanded files already exist in the target directory, first preserve this run's command output, then check where expansion ends in the output and whether the post hook text appears in the expected order. What needs to be confirmed is whether the post hook can still be seen in the same output after expansion completes. Don't only inspect files modified by the hook; file existence only shows that part of the expansion completed and cannot, by itself, show that the hook ran.

If the hook text appears before expansion ends, trace back through the integration-test entry at `tests/integration/hooks.rs` to inspect the assertions and test fixtures, and stop at the output-order layer first. If expanded files exist but this run left no post hook output, first record whether the target directory was produced by this generation run, and preserve the complete output. Then rerun the same local template input. If the hook still can't be observed on the second run, stop at the integration-test entry and leave it as "output missing" rather than rewriting it as a template-content error. If even the expanded files were not generated, return to the generation-failure investigation; this page does not replace that path.

## Anomalous inheritance in local template results

If the input comes from a local template directory, first record the directory actually used, the default-branch information in that directory, and representative generated files. First determine "which local content was obtained," then evaluate the value after Liquid expansion; don't directly apply the revision-selection approach for remote Git templates to a local directory.

If the local directory clearly shows a default branch but the generated result comes from another set of files, preserve the filenames and directory state on both sides, and return to the template-source selection layer. If the directory itself doesn't contain enough information to establish the default branch, stop and mark it as needing confirmation; don't infer the inheritance rule from the generated result, and don't generalize one success or failure to all local templates.

The two branches may both occur in the same test run, but keep them recorded separately: one record for the output order, and one for the local template source and result. The next review should still start from the local test entry at `tests/integration/hooks.rs`.

# Cargo Ancestor Environment Variables Migration Notes

This page did not originally start from a stable file entry point. The clues available to the investigator were the issue name "Cargo Ancestor Environment Variables" and several call names. Based on these clues, the old record landed on `src/template.rs`. Later, this clue needed to be migrated to a file location that could be rechecked, so the following set of location information was retained: `internal/CG`, `v_prev`, and `src/template.rs`. They are a post-migration reference entry point; they do not indicate that all call relationships have been confirmed.

## What the Old Entry Left Behind

The old page had only two valid points: the issue was indeed related to the environment before and after Cargo generation; searching for template and rendering terms at the time pointed to `src/template.rs`. The remaining judgments were not settled in this record. In particular, the old record did not provide enough code references to determine whether the ancestor environment variable was formed during template parsing, project writing, or some caller's preparation stage.

Therefore, the old entry cannot simply be renamed as the current conclusion. People revisiting it may still enter through the issue name to reach the old page, or open the file directly through a call name. Both entry points will be retained for a while; the page content only migrates the file location and the local information that has been checked, without disguising old guesses as an implementation description.

The local dependencies left at the time are copied here as-is so that subsequent readers know which section to start from:

```rust
use anyhow::{Context, Result};
use console::style;
use indicatif::{MultiProgress, ProgressBar};
use liquid::Parser;
```

These declarations help locate the code near template handling and progress output. They cannot by themselves prove where the Cargo variable is read, nor prove that the variable still exists after rendering. `Context` and `Result` indicate that errors return along the anyhow path; `Parser` indicates that the file header touches Liquid; `MultiProgress` and `ProgressBar` indicate that progress-related objects exist here. For now, this stops at the declaration level to avoid presenting the import relationships as a complete data flow.

## Review Order After Migration

```text
Old issue name / call name clues
          |
          v
internal/CG @ v_prev
          |
          v
Local declarations and adjacent code in src/template.rs
          |
          v
Record "observed phenomena" or retain unconfirmed items

The issue name is suitable for searching adjacent records, while the call name is suitable for returning to the code; even when both point to the same file, that does not mean the semantics on both sides are already consistent.

Second, fix the review on the `v_prev` version of `internal/CG`. The version number here belongs to the material used in the old investigation and cannot be replaced with the state of the code seen later. First confirm that the file is still `src/template.rs`, then inspect the file header and the directly adjacent implementation. If the path or local declarations have changed, record the difference separately; do not overwrite the old record with the new file contents.

Third, copy only fragments that can be directly verified in the file or test output. You may record variable names, read points, the object passed into the template, and the order in which they appear; write "unconfirmed" for anything not seen, and do not fill it in based on Cargo's general behavior. The purpose of this migration is not to reinterpret the template system, but to ensure that the next time someone enters through the issue name, they can return to the same old path material and know where the record stops.

Fourth, place caller results separately after the file location. If a caller reports only the generation result, that is insufficient to infer that `src/template.rs` is responsible for reading the variable; seeing a read point in the file is also insufficient to infer that all callers pass through it. When both exist, record them in the order "file excerpt—caller result" rather than combining the two pieces of evidence into an unverified causal chain.

## From Where to Where

The old path was a search driven by the issue name and call name. Its drawback was that similar Cargo phenomena could easily be grouped under the same filename. The new path is temporarily `src/template.rs` in the `v_prev` version of `internal/CG`, with local verification continuing in that file. Here, "new" only means that the record entry has become specific; it does not mean that the implementation has migrated.

If someone enters from the old page, they should first retain the old link, then change the location in the body to the following minimum information:

- Repository: `internal/CG`
- Version: `v_prev`
- File: `src/template.rs`
- Observation scope: file header declarations, the area near template parsing, and direct adjacent code related to Cargo

These four items are sufficient to restart a review. Do not casually fold other template files, callers, or configuration files in the project into this page; the current material does not list them or provide a confirmed relationship between them and the ancestor environment variable. When crossing files is necessary, leave the specific filename and the connection observed at the time on this page, rather than writing only "continue tracing calls."

The first migration handles only the entry point. First retain the text in the old page that points to `src/template.rs`, then add the version and file path. This batch does not determine whether the variable has already been consumed by Cargo, and it does not rewrite the old judgment.

The second review handles the local file content. # Decision record: usage errors for missing template parameters

In 0.14 Compatibility Train, "Missing Template Parameter Usage Error" is described inconsistently in two current documents. The observed results don't provide enough detail to treat either description directly as a regression finding; in particular, we cannot attribute the issue to either command-line parsing or template expansion just because the error is called usage.

## Entry points confirmed at the time

`src/main.rs` is the command-line entry point examined first in this round. The only direct adjacency at the top of the file is:

```rust
use cargo_generate::{generate, Cli};
use structopt::StructOpt;
```

This shows that command-line argument parsing and the handoff between `Cli` and `generate` are near the same entry point, but it does not establish that missing-value validation happens here. The earlier investigation pointed the issue name and call name to this file, making it a useful starting point for tracing where the usage text is assembled; this navigation hint should not be treated as establishing implementation ownership.

## Decisions made

For maintenance, initially treat this as "inconsistent classification of argument errors visible to users," rather than recasting it as "template parameters are definitely missing at a particular fixed stage." Materials that need updating should retain just one clear position: when a template parameter is missing, the command should produce an error that callers can recognize as usage, rather than continuing to target generation or mixing ordinary expansion failures into the same message.

The investigation will prioritize the command-line boundary. First record the triggering input, full error output, and where execution exits; then confirm whether the handoff from `Cli` to `generate` already carries that parameter. If the value has passed the entry point, further investigation should move to library-side template configuration and placeholder handling; if the entry point has already rejected the input, maintain the command-line usage text and argument documentation. Conclusions for one path must not be substituted for conclusions for the other.

The quality gate does not accept screenshots that only say "failed due to missing parameters." Regression records must at least distinguish: which template parameter is missing, whether the error is still usage, and whether any output directory or files were created before the failure. The last item is to prevent errors reported after partial generation from being misclassified as input validation.

## Materials to bring back for review

- A minimal template paired with invocation input that has a missing value;
- Verbatim error output, without trimming off the usage section;
- The actual handoff locations from the `src/main.rs` entry point to `Cli` and `generate`;
- If the target directory has already been written to, list the filenames that appeared first.

Until these materials are obtained, the maintenance page will not select either "parser issue" or "renderer issue" as the sole attribution. This decision preserves the current user-facing boundary without using the location of the entry-point file as a substitute for the actual call chain.

# Proposal for cloning without an SSH agent

This proposal was originally written for 0.14 Compatibility Train's interface review. People later continued to find it through the Local Clone Without SSH Agent issue. It records what was planned for trial at the time, not a set of authentication rules that had been implemented. The initial assessment treated "local source" and "no authentication required" as too closely related; the later review did not support conflating them.

## Original proposal retained

The original proposal started with a narrow case: the caller starts generation from a template source accessible on the local machine, but has no SSH agent. At the time, the assumption was that an identity file would be the easiest input for callers to specify, leading to the direction: "provide the path explicitly, check it before cloning, and don't silently guess a default identity."

Two approaches were compared at the time.

- **Explicit path first.** The caller provides an identity file. Expand home and normalize the path first; if it can't be used, stop rather than look for other files on the caller's behalf.
- **Search default locations when no path is provided.** If there is no path, try common locations, then pass the result to Git.

The original proposal favored the first approach, not because it had been proven more correct, but because its failure boundaries were easier to explain. The main concern with the second approach was not the implementation effort, but the tool selecting another identity when the caller had provided none. During later troubleshooting, it would be hard to tell whether a difference came from the template source, path interpretation, or default lookup.

The original proposal also included the line, "A local source that doesn't need an identity at all shouldn't go through this object." That remains as an old assumption, but must no longer be treated as a conclusion. Local accessibility only describes where the source is; it does not establish that subsequent Git operations will require no authentication or identity selection. Remote authentication policy was not covered in the proposal either. Trying to resolve both together would have distracted from the interface review.

## Later review

During a later reread of the relevant documentation against the then-current version, CG-217 led readers back to this page. The local entry point that could be confirmed was still `src/git/identity_path.rs`. The dependencies listed directly at the top of the file were:

```rust
use crate::git::utils::{canonicalize_path, home};
use anyhow::{bail, Result};
use std::path::{Path, PathBuf};
use std::fmt::{Display, Formatter};
```

This is enough to show that including path expansion, normalization, and display format in the same discussion at the time was not pure speculation. It does not prove when higher-level code constructs this object, nor that local template sources necessarily go through the same call chain. The original proposal made these uninvestigated parts sound too much like established relationships. That is a gap this review needs to keep visible.

After the review, the problem can be broken down into three smaller judgments: whether the caller explicitly provided an identity; whether the supplied value can be interpreted as a usable path; and whether generation actually needs identity handling when there is no explicit value. The first two belong near the identity path object. The third depends on source selection and the actual entry point for Git operations, and should not be replaced by a default file search.

## Reframing the options

If this trial continues, the recommendation is still to start with an explicit path, but to treat it as a reversible narrowing of the interface, not as "all local clones require an identity." When the caller explicitly provides a path, the identity path object handles expansion and normalization, and reports unusable paths at that boundary. This lets callers distinguish "I didn't provide an identity" from "the file I provided isn't usable."

Default lookup can remain as another candidate, provided the legacy calling scenario it serves is identified first. Without that scenario, files under home should not be scanned automatically just because the SSH agent is missing. In particular, default lookup must not be treated as a compatibility patch: it could mask a missing caller argument, or cause the same template to use different identities on different machines.

This page also need not prescribe standard wording for path display in advance. `Display` and `Formatter` appear nearby, which suggests that error readability is worth considering. But whether this object should handle the formatting, or a higher layer should add source information, still depends on the actual call sites. The earlier wording, "handle all error reporting here in one place," should be treated as draft language, not an implementation requirement.

The base directory for relative paths is still undecided. If paths are interpreted relative to the caller's working directory, embedded and command-line calls could produce different results; if they are always resolved against home or the template directory first, that would change the intuitive interpretation. This choice needs to wait until the higher-level entry point has been found; the import list in `identity_path.rs` cannot decide it.

## Withdrawal criteria and open items

If any of the following occurs, the "explicit identity path first" trial direction should be withdrawn and reassessed at the source entry point:

- The actual local-template path bypasses identity handling entirely;
- Identity is already determined at an earlier Git configuration layer, and passing it again would only create two levels of precedence;
- Legacy callers depend on default locations, and the scope of that dependency and the migration cost can be clearly described.

The unanswered questions are whether the same layer should distinguish between a missing identity and a nonexistent path; which directory relative paths should be based on; and whether failure occurs before any template files are written. The early guesses on this page are no substitute for verifying the last point in particular.

This page is retained for anyone who needs to trace the interface trade-offs made at the time. Further implementation judgments should start at the actual references to `src/git/identity_path.rs`, rather than treating the candidate proposals here as current behavior.

# Integration Testing Window Closeout Checklist

Trigger: When preparing to close the integration testing window, check only the exit actions, the last visible result, and the actions already completed on the adj-guide side. The relevant owner still signs off separately on whether the release succeeded.

1. Open `docs/adj-guide/release/guide-client-integration-exit-window-checklist.md` and find `SSH identity` in the record for this window. If no space has been set aside for the identity, don't continue the closeout or fill it in from memory.
2. After you see `VCS initialization`, first preserve the state as it is. Don't rerun generation just to clean up the directory. The directory left at closeout is more useful than a fresh green result.
3. If `Liquid expansion` hasn't appeared, stop here; don't mark the later hook, directory, or version control state as complete after the fact.
4. Keep the last visible result next to the original input. A single success line in the logs doesn't count; results compiled afterward can't replace what was seen the first time either.

For now, close out in this order: first remove the temporary entry point, then return the borrowed resources, then write any remaining failing samples back to their original locations. Before removing the entry point, check whether new requests are still entering the window. If new requests still come in after the entry point is removed, restore the entry point and stop closing the window; the restore action in the shared environment has not been tried in this window.

If no return window is documented for the borrowed resources, hold off on removal. Even if the results have been saved, if the resources haven't been returned, the window can only be recorded as not fully closed out. Keep the directory, input, and results in the same place so the person taking over doesn't see only the cleaned-up directory.

Don't treat closing the window as release approval. This is only for preserving the integration testing state; release decisions not listed here still go back to the original owner.

# Integration Window Exit Checklist

This checklist is still for a single integration window: closing out the call samples, adaptation boundaries, and integration feedback around example. It does not replace release sign-off. The old practice of cleaning out the directory before making an assessment is retained below, so anyone taking over can see why the window was mistakenly thought to be closed at the time.

When opening the window, record the current version, original input, and first visible result alongside `docs/adj-guide/release/guide-client-integration-exit-window-checklist.md`. The record doesn't need to explain every part of the generation process for the caller, but the input and result must be available to review together. A cleaned-up directory on its own is not enough to tell whether it came from this window.

## What to Keep When Opening the Window

- [ ] Keep one sample of the success path and one of the rejection path; don't overwrite the first result with a green result produced by later cleanup.
- [ ] Record the return window for any borrowed accounts, workers, environments, or proxies. Leave resources without a recorded return window in place for now.
- [ ] If the setup depends on `SSH identity`, record where it is used in this window's record; "already configured" alone is not enough for a handoff.
- [ ] Keep the original input, generated directory, and last visible result in the same record. If the directory has no corresponding result before cleanup, add the result location first; don't start cleanup.

The rejection path is not there to prove that the release failed. It only records where the caller in this window cannot proceed. If the setup was temporarily changed for diagnosis, that result and the original sample must not be combined into one entry; success after cleanup must not be backfilled as though the original run had already succeeded.

## Old Window-Closing Procedure

1. After seeing `VCS initialization`, delete the generated directory and temporary logs.
2. If `Liquid expansion` has appeared, mark the template source selector as passed.
3. Revoke temporary permissions, remove bypasses, and confirm that the queue is no longer accepting new work.

These three actions were once treated as the complete exit criteria. The problem with that approach is that deleting the directory also removes the last visible result, and seeing expansion does not establish that the caller received the artifact they needed to inspect. This has not been replaced with a new release standard; the old sequence is retained for reviewing past windows.

The old sequence has another practical consequence: when removing the entry point is written as the last step, someone taking over can easily check only whether the entry point is gone, without recording whether there were still requests before it was removed. Without that record, if the entry point is reopened later, there is no way to tell whether it is a restoration or a new round of integration testing.

## Actual Checks Before Closing the Window

- [ ] Look at the artifact or status first, then at "success" in the logs. Don't mark the template source selector as passed if no artifact has been retained.
- [ ] Before revoking permissions, confirm that no new requests are still entering this window. If you can't confirm that, leave the entry point in place and stop closing the window.
- [ ] Record unfinished items under someone who can continue the work, or in their original location; "the project team will keep an eye on it" does not count as a handoff.
- [ ] For cases that go beyond the current caller interface, don't expand the investigation on the fly. Stop and hand them back to the corresponding entry point.

If you find that requests are still coming in after removing the entry point, restore the original entry point first and preserve the result from that time. Don't replace what was observed with a green result from a rerun. The restoration has not yet been rerun in the shared environment; therefore, "looks normal after restoration" cannot be retroactively recorded as a verified exit criterion.

When taking over, still start from that path. What can be handed over here is the samples, entry point status, and resource return windows; this checklist does not determine whether the release succeeded.

# Integration Testing Window Exit Checklist

What was first seen is the easiest thing to lose when the window ends. Caller-side integration testing has left behind generated directories, expansion logs, and temporary entry points; cleanup usually outpaces the results. This checklist has always recorded only exit actions, the last visible result, and the actions of adj-guide itself; release sign-off is not part of this checklist.

Early records put "expansion seen" and "directory cleared" on the same line. The sequence at the time was: see `VCS initialization`, confirm `Liquid expansion`, delete the generated directory, then remove the temporary entry point. Anyone taking over could treat it as "window closed" simply by seeing these items in the live setup.

This sequence has not been removed. It still explains why old windows left gaps: once the directory was cleared, the first visible result and original input were no longer at hand; a later successful run could not fill the original slot either. Likewise, "template source selector passed" in the old records was only a judgment made at the time, not an indication that all callers received the same result.

The old approach also assumed that no new requests would arrive once the entry point was removed. The checklist provided no place to verify this assumption, so "closed" in past records sometimes meant only that cleanup was complete, not that the caller-side visible result had been saved. This passage is retained not so that the approach can continue to be used; someone taking over an old window may still encounter records like these first.

## Preparation That Can Still Be Done As Before

- [ ] Start with `docs/adj-guide/release/guide-client-integration-exit-window-checklist.md`, and retain the current version, original input, and first visible result.
- [ ] Retain one sample each for the success path and the rejection path. Keep the samples separate from the cleaned-up directories; cleanup happens after recording is complete.
- [ ] Any borrowed account, worker, environment, or proxy must still have a return window specified. Do not remove the resource without a return window.
- [ ] When `SSH identity` is used in the live setup, specify which section it appears in. Do not retroactively label records without an identity location as "confirmed".
- [ ] If the generated directory already exists, only indicate its relationship to the current input; do not delete the directory and create a new one just to make the sample complete.

A success sample only shows that a viewable result was retained this time. A rejection sample likewise only shows where the caller stopped at the time. Neither substitutes for a release conclusion, and they certainly should not be overwritten with logs compiled later. If diagnosis changes the entry point, permissions, or directory, record the post-change output separately; it cannot be treated as the first result from when the window opened.

The preparation items above come from supplementary notes for old windows, not universal release criteria. In particular, record a worker or proxy only if it was borrowed for this caller-side integration testing session; if nothing was borrowed, do not add an item just to fill out the checklist. The same applies to accounts and environments: what is recorded is the return window, not a judgment about their long-term state.

## Stop Points on Exit

1. First capture the last visible result. It should sit directly beside the original input for this run, rather than being a "success" statement extracted from logs compiled later. If the original input is missing, record the gap first and stop cleanup.
2. Next, check whether new requests are still arriving before removing the entry point. If this cannot be determined, retain the entry point and stop closing the window; do not turn "none seen for now" into confirmation that there are no requests.
3. If new requests appear after temporary permissions and bypasses have been removed, restore the original entry point and retain the result from that moment; do not replace it with a green result from a rerun.
4. If an account, worker, environment, or proxy to be returned has no specified return window, do not remove it yet. A recorded return window does not mean the resource has been returned; the return action must still remain in the original record.
5. Stop here on any item that requires going beyond the caller interface to answer. Leave unfinished items in their original locations, and do not expand them into release investigation within the window.

The recovery actions still have not been rerun in the shared environment. The old version listed "remove the entry point" as the definite final step; this may make things easier when there are no new requests, but it cannot establish the state after removal or replace release sign-off. Whether the window needs to be closed again after restoring the entry point is also not something the old procedure on this page can answer.

## Most Recent Review

The counterexample in CGA-003 exposed the flaw in the old check: the internal results contained the current result, but the regular entry point corresponding to the exit entry point did not. What was subsequently written back was the fact that "the regular entry point lacks the current result"; the internal results are no longer included in the same acceptance check.

Therefore, when closing this window, do not combine the internal results and regular entry point results into one passing item. If the regular entry point lacks the current result, record the absence itself and keep the window stopped; the internal results can still serve as evidence from the live setup, but cannot be used to mark the result as already visible at the regular entry point. This adjustment affects only how exit records are kept, and draws no conclusion about release status.

- [ ] If the regular entry point has the result for this run, retain that result and the location where it first became visible.
- [ ] If the regular entry point does not have the result for this run, state that it is missing, and do not substitute the internal results.
- [ ] If the result at the regular entry point was compiled later, still record it separately from the first visible result, and do not merge them into a single acceptance check.
- [ ] After the entry point has been removed, check once more for new requests; if there are any, restore the entry point and preserve the original state.

Here, the "regular entry point" is the usual route corresponding to the exit entry point, not another name for the internal results. The internal results can help show what was seen in the system at the time, but cannot fill the gap left by the regular entry point lacking the current result. If an old window saved only internal results, treat it as missing the regular entry point result; there is no need to regenerate a directory to fill the gap.

CGA-011 still records only the borrower, start time, and return window for the current revision. It provides no evidence that "the resource has been returned" and cannot be checked off as complete on this page. If a resource is about to be removed during the window but the card only lists a return window, retain the resource or refer the item back to the original record; do not treat the scheduled time as an action actually performed.

CGA-018 requires recovering the full command used at the time; once the parameters are complete, add a separate line rather than rewriting the old sample's input. Until the full command is recovered, the old sample can still show what was seen at the time, but cannot confirm parameters that were not recorded. A new command should not replace this gap either: a new invocation belongs to a new run.

## Old Notes, Not Yet Removed

The statement "the window can be closed as soon as `Liquid expansion` is seen" remains in the early paragraphs. It is useful for quickly judging how far the process has progressed, but not for judging whether the regular entry point is visible. Another old statement says the live setup can be cleaned up after VCS initialization; this would deprive whoever takes over of the original input and first result, so it is no longer treated as a priority action at this stage.

The template source selector's output can remain in the sample, but if there is no output, logs alone cannot be used to mark it as passed. If the old procedure has already deleted the generated directory, record only the gap; do not generate another directory just to complete the checklist. A new directory belongs to a new run, and can neither restore the old window's first result nor prove that the old entry point was already visible at the time.

The old checklist placed "entry point removed" and "resource returned" very close together, making the two look like the same action. They are still recorded separately now: whether the entry point is still receiving new requests, and whether a borrowed resource has reached its return window, are two different checks. If either cannot be confirmed, leave it at the stop point on this page, without expanding into a release judgment on the fly.

A related question still sits outside the window: this checklist has not yet determined when the temporary entry point may be removed after the regular entry point is found to lack the current result. For now, handle this as a stop point until someone takes over the corresponding entry point.

The preference was for the latter; in the old draft, the two flows had different failure exits. With both behind a single entry point, it was hard to tell from the logs whether things had stopped at directory handling or configuration selection.

Whether rollback would only restore the old entry point had not been decided at the time. # Integration Testing Entry Point Migration Index

This index covers entry point changes for guide-client-integration, not all template behavior. Only actual call samples, adaptation boundaries, and integration feedback produced around example may be included. Pages with similar names in the directory are not automatically included; notes for which no caller can be found or whose original location cannot be revisited remain as outdated records.

The current entry point file is still `docs/adj-guide/migration/current-entry-legacy-entry-migration-index.md`. It is both the starting point for review and the place where old and new records sit side by side. The old entry point does not disappear just because a replacement location exists; it cannot be described as taken offline while callers are still using it, the exit action has not yet been mapped to the actual adj-guide, or the environment has changed and comparison with the old results in the same round is no longer possible.

First, classify each row in the index into the following four categories. Here, a "caller" means a specific integration that actually uses guide-client-integration, not a page that merely mentions the entry point in the directory.

| Row type | What the old record should retain | What the current index should add | When migration cannot continue |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Caller still in use | Original entry point name, known inputs, and first visible result | A record of the same call under the current revision | The set of callers is based only on guesswork or screenshots |
| Caller with an existing replacement location | Why the original entry point is still retained | Replacement location and adaptation boundaries | The replacement location is evidenced only by a filename |
| Exit action | Original exit action and what it points to | The actual adj-guide corresponding to that action | The action maps only to a page color or directory status |
| Old notes that cannot be traced back | Original text and its context at the time | An outdated marker, without fabricating a conclusion | No original input, version, or failure exit |

```text
Old entry point record ──────────────> Current index
      │                         │
      │ Preserve the original failure exit           │ Migrate only confirmed callers
      ▼                         ▼
Exit action ──────────────> Actual adj-guide

The existence of a replacement location does not mean the old entry point can be deleted
```

The earliest record treated the issue as a choice between `init mode` and splitting out the `placeholder value`. That was a judgment made during the work, not a list of names for current operations. The two records have different failure exits, showing that entry point text and actual calls can no longer be maintained together as if they were the same thing. The old paragraph is still retained: it reminds whoever takes over that the earlier comparison did not confirm the callers currently using `post hook`, nor did it answer whether reverting means restoring only the old entry point. Subsequent migration work should not rewrite these unanswered questions as if they had been resolved.

## Before Migration Begins

Select an actual call sample from the current index, rather than a set of notes that looks newer. First, copy down the current entry point used by that call, the original input, the observed failure result, and the version at the time. Here, the version means version information that can identify this particular call; a verbal description saying only that it "was run recently" cannot replace a record. Retain the original input together with the first visible result; successful screenshots compiled later must not overwrite them.

Next, confirm whether this sample still belongs to guide-client-integration. Samples produced through example can be included in this index; material that merely mentions the same term elsewhere but has no integration feedback stays where it is. This restriction is practical: the migration index needs to determine whether a call can switch entry points, not explain every template setting for peripheral projects.

Before switching environments, export the current guide-client-integration together with its exit action. The archiving requirement in CGA-021 comes from this point: after the environment changes, the old and new results can no longer be called a comparison from the same round. Exporting does not declare the migration complete; it only preserves the entry point, call, and exit status at the time for later review. If the export is missing an item, first mark the gap beside the original step, then continue investigating; do not fill it in using adjacent pages.

## Handling the Old Entry Point

The old entry point must retain at least two types of information: how it is called, and what the consumer can see when it fails. The former prevents treating the index as a mere directory migration, while the latter prevents the replacement location from retaining only successful results. For callers still using it, keep the old entry point readable for now; if the replacement location is still being tried out, the old entry point is also the destination needed for a revert.

Do not interpret "old" as no longer in use. A caller Fang Ke may already be able to find the current index, but its exit action may still point back to the old object; alternatively, the entry point text may have been replaced, but there may be no corresponding operation for the actual adj-guide. The requirement in CGA-014 to trace back along the exit action to the actual object is intended to rule out these two forms of apparent completion. If it cannot be traced back, the status in the index should be "Pending trace-back", not "Migrated".

CGA-006 added a requirement for reproduction by a second person: the person reproducing the procedure follows the steps using only the materials already on the card, and notes anything they cannot find directly beside the original step. This approach is suitable for pre-migration checks. It distinguishes two kinds of gaps: one where the index is unclear, and another where the old entry point never had reusable call materials in the first place. The former can be addressed with additional explanation; for the latter, the only option is to retain the old record and pause that caller's migration.

A second person's ability to reach the replacement location does not automatically mean the old entry point can be deleted. The entry point and input they used, along with the visible result, still need to be put back into the same row for comparison. If they can proceed only by relying on additional verbal background or temporary links elsewhere, the index still does not provide a migration record that can be handed off.

## How to Document Replacement Locations

For a replacement location, record only which call it has taken over; do not describe it as an umbrella term for all entry points. The early comparison considered splitting out the `placeholder value` as a candidate direction; if a call later uses a different location, state which old record it replaces rather than overwriting the old judgment. This is the only way to tell whether a call has completed its move or merely gained another set of notes.

At a minimum, append a migration record in this order: first retain the old entry point's status; then document the replacement location; next include the consumer's actual result; finally state whether the exit action now points to the actual adj-guide. This order is not a formatting requirement, but a way to prevent "a replacement location exists" from being misread as "the caller has already migrated". If any one of these items is unclear, the row can remain incomplete.

Old and new conclusions need to sit side by side, rather than silently changing the old sentences. CGA-007 requires marking the context of the old judgment before appending new guide-client-integration results. For the index, the old judgment preserves why the entry point was not split up at the time; the new conclusion preserves which call has been confirmed by the current materials. If the two conflict, identify the call or exit action where the conflict occurs, rather than hiding the difference with a simple "Updated".

Some old notes cannot be traced back. They are still useful: readers can see that an entry point was once mentioned, while avoiding treating that mention as new evidence of a call. Do only two things with these notes: retain their original location, and mark them as outdated. Do not infer their inputs and results at the time from adjacent documents, similar names, or calls that succeeded later.

## Small-Batch Migration

Batch the migration by caller, not by directory. Each batch moves only consumers that can already be confirmed; the remaining rows stay under the old entry point. The reason is not to pursue a uniform release cadence, but that calls on the same page may have different failure exits, replacement locations, and exit actions. If they are switched together, once differences appear, it will be impossible to know which old record to return to.

At the start of a batch, keep guide-client-integration, the current entry point, and the command used fixed, changing only the current revision. CGA-022 defines this condition narrowly, and the index should keep the comparison equally narrow: do not change the entry point text, environment, and version at the same time and then call the result migration validation. If the result differs after the current revision changes, first record the difference against this row; decide separately whether to use the replacement location.

If a failure occurs in a small batch, first check whether it can still be reproduced through the old entry point. If it can, retain the old entry point and record that the replacement location did not handle this call; if it cannot, do not rush to classify it as a replacement-location issue, but first check whether the environment has already switched. A sample from a changed environment that was not exported beforehand can only be treated as a new observation; it cannot be used alongside results from the old round to draw conclusions.

At the end of each batch, check whether three things match: the caller documented in the index, the call actually handled by the replacement location, and the actual adj-guide pointed to by the exit action. Confirm the first using consumer-provided materials, trace back the second from the current entry point, and trace back the third along the exit action. If any one of these three links is broken, the batch remains in progress; the old entry point continues to be retained.

## Rollback

Rollback does not mean deleting the current index, but routing this call through the old entry point again while retaining the result of this replacement attempt. First restore the old entry point to a readable state, then run one check using the original input retained before migration. If the visible result after restoration differs from the pre-migration result, record the difference rather than classifying it as "Rollback successful". This may be caused by the current revision, environmental changes, or incomplete old materials; stop here if the existing index does not contain enough material.

When the replacement location does not match the original call, returning to the old entry point is an option; however, this does not justify concluding that other callers should also be rolled back together. Each call's exit action must be traced back independently. In particular, when the old entry point still has consumers and the replacement location covers only some samples, deleting the old entry point will leave later users without a recovery path.

The minimum state for a completed revert is: the original call can find the old entry point, the exit action can be mapped to the actual adj-guide, and the index retains the replacement location and result of this attempt. If only the page text has been restored, without restoring the entry point used by Fang Ke, this counts as incomplete. The earlier question of "whether to restore only the old entry point" remains unresolved; do not turn it into a universal rule without new call materials.

## Review and Maintenance

Review starts from the current index file, not from a similarly named alternate route. CGA-006 can be used to arrange for a second person to retrace the original steps; CGA-007 is used to retain old and new conclusions; CGA-014 is used to check exit actions; CGA-021 handles archiving before an environment switch; CGA-022 constrains the current revision comparison to a single variable. These cards provide navigation only; they do not replace the call records in the index.

DOC-27 can help locate nearby call contexts, but it does not determine which entry point here has already been migrated. Index maintainers should append only consumers, replacement locations, and exit actions they can trace back themselves. Rows that cannot be confirmed remain outdated until new actual call samples appear.

The final check is not about whether the directory is tidy, only whether the old entry point, new location, and actual calls still correspond one to one. If they do not, it is better to leave the old entry point and the gaps in place than to label a partial trial as a full migration.
versions.change_summary: Complete the batch migration, rollback, and review index

# Release Automation User FAQ

This page covers only three questions users may encounter when trying to find the right entry point, revision, or owner. It covers the release process in `.github/workflows`, the build queue it creates, and artifacts that have already been produced or are due to be withdrawn. example templates · Release Automation has its own schedule, maintainers, and exit criteria; don't apply the main project's status directly to it.

**Where is the entry point?**

Start at `docs/adj-example-templates/faq/example-templates-release-automation-three-user-questions.md`. The page and attachments are still maintained by `adj-example-templates`. If you see similar names, use this path and the actual workflow as the reference first; don't rely on the page title alone to decide whether it's the same release process.

**What is the current revision?**

A verifiable revision isn't available here yet. The gap recorded in CGB-013 is that the current revision from the second run or read wasn't retained, and the available material only shows the final state. The final artifact version therefore cannot be treated as the input version used by the workflow. The revision read at runtime, the corresponding minimal input, and the result's position in the build queue need to be added. Without these fields, the withdrawal window can only be handled based on existing artifact records; the missing run cannot be inferred by working backward.

**Who do we hand off to if the release gets stuck?**

Keep it on the example templates · Release Automation side first, with the maintainer on duty determining whether it is still within this project's scope based on the workflow, queue position, and artifact version. If the withdrawal window is still open, CGB-014 requires saving the minimal input, version, and withdrawal action first; the original owner must also be contacted before the window expires, as specified in CGB-007. If it crosses into a shared interface, handing over the reproduction entry point and observed behavior is enough; don't transfer the entire schedule along with it. The reproduction agreement in CGB-020 is for a second colleague to reproduce the issue using only the material on the original card and note anything missing beside the original steps. Revisions that remain unconfirmed are not filled in here by guesswork.

# Troubleshooting tree for stalled release automation

When release automation stalls at the current entry point, first preserve the state still visible there, then follow the branches below. Here, "stalled" only means that the queue has not progressed to producing an artifact version, or that no next step has been provided before the withdrawal window; don't fold other template issues into this.

## Check the template configuration first

Find the corresponding template configuration via `docs/adj-example-templates/runbooks/example-templates-release-automation-escalation-when-blocked.md`. If you can confirm that the configuration is still there, continue along the example-templates-release-automation branch; if you can't find the configuration itself, stop troubleshooting and leave the entry point location for the person who maintains that configuration.

When you see `pre hook`, don't clear the existing state. The old process treated the queue states before and after the hook as a single record: if the entry point still shows that the hook has been entered, but there is no new artifact version, hand it off to the release automation maintainer and include the segment of state visible at the entry point. Don't take this to mean that the hook ran successfully, and don't start withdrawal prematurely.

If the template configuration specifies `sub-template root`, but that root does not appear at the current entry point, stop here. This branch was often treated as a release queue issue in the past, but work can only proceed once the template configuration side provides evidence of the root selection. Without that evidence, don't move to the artifact version or withdrawal window branches.

## When there are no configuration anomalies

If the configuration and `pre hook` both line up, but the queue still hasn't produced an artifact version, first check whether you can still open the normal access path from the current entry point.

- The normal entry point opens: hand the issue back to example-templates-release-automation. The handoff should state only "configuration visible, queue has not progressed," without a final cause.
- The normal entry point denies access: stop at the permissions entry point. Record where the denial occurs; this is not evidence of a problem with the template contents. The person with permission to access that entry point decides whether to investigate further.
- An artifact version has already appeared: stop using this tree to investigate the template root. If it is still within the withdrawal window, leave the decision on whether to withdraw to the release automation side; this page provides no recovery steps.

This procedure preserves the entry point breakdown used at the time. It assumes you start with the template configuration, then check `pre hook` and the subtemplate root; if there are multiple symptoms, still follow only the branch for which evidence was obtained first. Entry points, queue information, or permissions pages added later have not been incorporated.

Recovery actions have not been tested in the shared environment. If actual recovery is needed, first make a separate record of the artifact version and withdrawal window at that time, then decide whether to use the handoff approach described here.
