# Template Variables Two-Record Incident Postmortem

The two revisions of adj-template-variables still landed at the same entry point. In v1, the difference was initially attributed to project-name normalization; that assessment later turned out to be insufficient. During review, the template source selector itself was still working, but the comparison pointed to a local-path template. Therefore, the entire change cannot be explained by looking only at the project name ultimately displayed at the entry point.

## Incident Extract

| Time | Observed phenomenon | Action taken |
|---|---|---|
| T+00 | `template-variables-dependency-boundary-audit-two-record-versions-not-merged` first diverged from the original revision | Save the original input and entry-point version |
| T+07 | The template source selector was still working normally | Narrow the investigation to differences in source selection and before/after expansion |
| T+18 | The comparison pointed to a local-path template | Route the branch back through the corresponding maintenance entry point |
| T+31 | The user path recovered | Record recovery separately from root-cause confirmation |

The relationship sketched at the time was short:

```text
consumer -> template-variables-dependency-boundary-audit-two-record-versions-not-merged -> template source selector -> local-path template
              ^ Compare only the first change
```

The earlier screenshot-only retelling did not preserve the revision or input location, so it could not later explain why the other path worked. By preserving the original state this time, the two versions and the entry point can at least be viewed together. There is no evidence that the local-path template was the root cause, and no evidence that project-name normalization was completely unrelated.

### Differences found during review

The template configuration, Liquid expansion, and hook ordering were not merged across the two record versions. One review saw the pre hook first; another saw the post hook first. Both show that the expansion process is more than simply copying the template tree, but this does not establish that every hook ran during this deviation. `progress boundary` was also recorded separately: when green output appears, the visibility of the subsequent post hook still needs to be confirmed.

The "template test command" was kept as a suspected change rather than treated as a confirmed cause. The offline build evidence was not completed. Working-directory restoration and the generated target directory were also included in the scope of follow-up checks, because after the project name was overridden by the init hook, the target directory and Template Variables might no longer be calculated from the initial input; that was only the working assumption at the time.

The sub-template root was another adjacent difference. If a child template is selected in the configuration, comparison should first confirm the template root actually selected; it must not directly treat the contents of the parent template tree as the output source. This observation did not explain why the two revisions landed at the same entry, so it was not written up as the root cause at the time.

`placeholder value` only indicates that an unreplaced value appeared during expansion. The existing records do not trace it back to a specific input, nor do they prove that it is necessarily related to the project name or revision. It was left as part of the state to preserve during a later review, not as proof of successful recovery.

### Recovery and object identity

The recovery action was to preserve the entry-point version, stop further overwrites, and return to a usable state using the overwrite operation that was already working. The recovered user path did not pin down the root cause. The process stopped at the current interface boundary; the unreproduced branch remains to be investigated. Do not delete the earlier records for DOC-40; place new differences in subsequent versions.

The archive for CGC-001 notes that the object sharing the name of `template-variables-supply-boundary` needs an explicit version label. CGC-017 later confirmed that the object was usable, but the fork after the current entry still needs to be handed off to the maintainer. The two cards show that the object identity and maintenance entry point have changed; they cannot replace the contemporaneous record of this incident.

The records for CGC-018 document the approach of tracing execution records to the first broken link and stopping at the result available at that time. This approach changed the review order: instead of looking only at the last line of green output, the location of the first broken link must be retained. It did not turn the output before the break into a success.

The rerun approach recorded in CGC-019 is to keep `template-variables-supply-boundary`, the current entry point, and the command fixed, replacing only the current revision. This approach is consistent with the anomaly on this page, but this version has no rerun result, so it is not marked as verified.

### Questions still unanswered at the time

- How to label the revisions separately for two same-named objects.
- Who will continue maintaining the fork after the current entry point, and when the old entry point will be retired.
- Whether the template test command actually ran in this path, and whether it affected the output.
- The selection order among the sub-template root, the parent template tree, and the local-path template.
- Whether the post hook produced output after the progress boundary that the screenshot missed.
- The actual changes to the target directory and `placeholder value` after project-name normalization.

The user path has been restored, but no single record has yet fully explained the relationship among object identity, template source, and the expansion process.

# Template Variables Dual-Record Incident Postmortem

adj-template-variables placed the current revision for two revisions under the same entry point for a time. This wording comes from the earliest incident observations, not a summary compiled later. The first observation was that project name normalization was inconsistent with the old records; only later was it discovered that the template source selector still worked, while the content being compared had switched to a local-path template. After that, the hook, template test command, generation target directory, and caller-side regression testing each left traces. These were different observations from the same round of anomalies, not enough to combine into a single confirmed root cause.

This page therefore preserves three levels: what was first observed, how the scope of comparison was narrowed along the way, and which issues remained unverified after recovery. Later records cannot retroactively replace earlier assessments.

## The Evidence Recorded First

v1 contained only a few lines at the time. The first observed difference was that project name normalization differed from the old records. The original entry point `docs/adj-template-variables/incidents/template-variables-dependency-boundary-audit-two-unmerged-record-versions.md` was retained, and further retries were halted. That version considered overwriting sufficient for recovery, but did not answer why the template test command had changed.

These few sentences were not deleted later. They serve two purposes: preserving the bias in the initial assessment, and preserving the gap left by the missing timestamp at the time. "Missing timestamp: ____" remains, because no material can turn this blank into a reliable timestamp. Filling it in with T+00, T+07, or any other time would backfill the earliest record with the later timeline.

The early sketch showed only relationships between objects, not a complete execution sequence:

```text
Two revisions
      |
      v
Same entry point ——> Template source selector ——> Expansion / hook ——> Output project
   |                              |
   +------ Current revision ----------+
```

The diagram above is not a call graph. It only indicates that the comparison point may have shifted among the entry point, source selection, and output at the time. The only objects actually recorded were the entry point, source selector, expansion process, and output project. Commands, parameters, and execution order that were not recorded must not be inferred from the diagram.

At the time, someone put "project name normalization" first because it was the most obvious surface-level difference from the old records. This working hypothesis was never fully ruled out later: after the init hook overwrites the project name, the target directory may change, and Template Variables may also be recalculated. But it never explained on its own why two revisions shared the same entry point, nor did it explain why a local-path template appeared in the comparison results.

## How the Incident Was Observed

T+00, `template-variables-dependency boundary audit-the two record versions have not been merged` first diverged from the original revision. The entry-point version and original input were saved first, and no immediate rerun was performed. Stopping retries was not a recovery action, but simply prevented a second result from overwriting the first set of material available for comparison.

T+07, the template source selector was still working normally. This result weakened the assessment that "the entry point had completely failed", but did not explain why two revisions could still appear at the same entry point. The comparison was therefore narrowed to the first point of change: whether the source selection had changed, and which template tree was used after selection. Here, "still working normally" applies only to this observation, not to the subsequent expansion and output.

T+18, the comparison pointed to a local-path template. This result meant that the initial attribution to the project name was incomplete. The project name could still affect the target directory, but it could not by itself explain why the source had already resolved to a local path. The corresponding branch was routed back to the maintenance entry point, and speculation about neighboring projects was not recorded as a cause at the time.

T+31, the user path was restored. The recovery time was recorded separately, and confirmation of the root cause was not announced along with the recovery. The green output in the old records could only show that a particular result was usable, not that the two revisions had been merged, nor that the same input would produce the same result later. Availability after recovery and entry-point identity are two separate matters.

This timeline does not include specific commands, accounts, or run IDs, because they were not preserved in the original material. In later reviews, the entry point and object names can be used for lookup, but the timeline cannot be used to invent a complete reproduction.

## Why the first attribution was weakened

The earliest records focused on project-name normalization. This did not come out of nowhere: once the init hook overrides the project name, the target directory changes, and Template Variables may also be recalculated. However, a local-path template, a pre hook, and a post hook were all present in the later observations, indicating that there were at least several adjacent nodes from source selection through completion of expansion. Attributing all of them to the project name would obscure the boundaries that actually needed to be compared.

v2 added the observation that "the template source selector was still working normally". It did not prove that the source selection result was correct, only that the selector had run through successfully at some point. The local-path template that appeared next also did not prove that this branch was the sole cause. Taken together, the two observations were enough to reject the claim that "looking only at the entry-point name can explain all the changes", but not enough to replace it with another definitive attribution.

Another premature judgment was to treat the "change in the test command" as a result of changes to the template content. The available records can only establish that the two versions of the record describe the template test command differently, not that the command was executed during every generation, nor that it rewrote the output. It remains an unconfirmed item and should not be recorded as a result in the postmortem.

Output order also caused another misreading. On site, someone saw green output appear near completion of the expansion and took it to mean that the entire process had ended. A later addendum distinguished the progress boundary from the post hook: if the post hook ran only after the progress boundary, looking only at the preceding output line would miss the subsequent results. This observation explains why the screenshot retelling was insufficient, but it does not prove that the post hook caused revisions to be mixed.

Liquid expansion, template configuration, and placeholder values also cannot be strung into a single causal chain. They appeared at different points in the review; the `placeholder value` indicates that a variable did not receive its expected substitution, but there is no corresponding input or expansion stage. The current material does not allow the unreplaced value to be traced to any one of the project name, revision, or hook.

## Comparison preserved by the intermediate version

v2 added a short timeline and also mapped the source branches. It did not attribute all differences to the same cause. The table below preserves the comparison points from that time; it is not a checklist designed later.

| Comparison point | Result observed on site | What it can show | What it cannot show |
|---|---|---|---|
| Entry | Two revisions were in the same place | The comparison position was unstable | It cannot show which revision should be the current version |
| Source selector | T+07 was still normal | At least part of the selection flow after entry was usable | It cannot show that the selected tree was necessarily correct |
| Local path template | T+18 appeared in the comparison result | This branch entered the local path template | It cannot prove that the path branch was the sole root cause |
| Project-name normalization | Inconsistent with the old record | The target directory and variables may have been recalculated | It cannot by itself explain the source change |
| Hook | The pre hook and post hook were seen in sequence | The expansion process includes pre- and post-actions | It cannot infer successful execution from the output order |
| Template test command | The two versions use different notation | Test-related behavior needs to be rechecked | Without an execution record, the result cannot be confirmed |
| sub-template root | Listed as an adjacent selection point | The selected subtemplate may determine the template tree | It cannot show that it caused the entry points to be mixed |
| Placeholder value | Appeared in the expansion review | A variable did not receive its expected value | It cannot be traced to a specific input or stage |

The asymmetry in the table must be preserved. The source selector has one on-site observation of "still normal," while the local path template has only a comparison reference, not complete success and failure samples. The hook's ordering was observed, but there was no per-step execution return. The template test command differs only in notation, with no run result. Filling all these columns out to the same level of completeness would create evidence that does not exist.

That screenshot-only retelling was later compared against the original entry. A screenshot can preserve one output line, but not the revision, input location, or before-and-after relationship, so it cannot explain why the other path worked normally. Keeping the original entry version is more useful than reorganizing the screenshot; the cleaned-up green output cannot overwrite the original scene.

## Source, template root and output location

The focus of the review later shifted from "whether the project name had changed" to "which template tree was actually selected". When sub-template is configured, first confirm whether the selected subtemplate is the template root, rather than assuming that the parent template tree is the output source. This determination only constrains the order of comparison, and is not a fix already completed for this incident.

A local-path template appeared in the comparison results at T+18. This shows that at least one input path led into a local-path template at the time. It does not tell us which revision selected that path, nor why the entry-point record retained both versions at the same time. The incident postmortem can retain this branch, but should not treat "local path" as a universal answer.

Changes to the target directory caused by overriding the project name must also be preserved separately. If the init hook changes the project name to another value, the old directory and the normalized directory cannot be lumped together as a single output location. Template Variables may be recalculated based on the target location, and a `placeholder value` may appear at one of these stages, but the existing records do not connect these two observations.

This is also why v2 included "restoring the working directory" and "generating the target directory" in the scope of the review. They concern adjacent boundaries involving the output location and the invocation environment, and do not confirm the root cause. Without records of the actual directories, we can only retain the direction of comparison, not fill in directory names or execution commands.

## hook and output order

The early screenshots treated a line of green output near the completion of expansion as the endpoint. Later supplementary notes showed that pre hook and post hook appeared separately in the records, so the progress boundary cannot automatically mean that all subsequent actions have finished. The review therefore needs to distinguish three points: the end marker of the expansion process, where the progress boundary appears, and whether post hook output is still visible afterward.

This distinction only addresses the question of "which section of output to look at". It does not show that the post hook necessarily ran, nor that the post hook modified the template content, still less that it changed the revision selection. If only screenshots from before the progress boundary are visible, the status of the post hook remains unknown.

Likewise, whether the template test command ran cannot be inferred from the word "test" appearing on the page. v2 retained it as a suspected change because the descriptions in the two versions of the records were inconsistent; v3 continues to retain this gap because no new execution records have been added. Offline build evidence and caller-side regression testing can also only serve as incomplete follow-up material, and cannot be used to prove the scope of recovery.

## Recovery actions did not extend to a redesign

Three concrete actions were taken during recovery: preserving the original entry-point version, stopping further overwrites, and returning to the overwrite-based write path that was already working. The sole purpose was to restore the user path and preserve the originals for comparison. Recovery did not clear out the two old revisions, nor did it turn the current entry point into a new long-term entry point.

The statement "overwriting can restore operation" remains in the old paragraph, but it only describes a single recovery observation at the time. It does not specify which target location was overwritten, nor whether the same revision was still used after recovery. Treating it as a general rule would go beyond the material left by this incident.

After recovery was complete, no announcement was made that the root cause had been confirmed. The user path was usable, but only the blocker preventing use at the time had been resolved; object version identification, separation of same-named objects, forks beyond the current entry point, and a single-variable rerun remained unresolved. The old record continued to be referenced because it preserved the sequence of events around the first deviation and the reasons for stopping retries, not because it had become the new unified operations page.

If two revision values are seen at the entry point again, the on-site sequence should still be to save the original, halt overwrites, and then check the source selector. If the source selector is still working normally, continue comparing the selected template tree; if the result leads to a local-path template, record that branch and the revision at the time. If only green output before the progress boundary is visible, do not treat it as confirmation that the post hook has completed. Even after the user path is restored, retain the results from before recovery.

## Object Identity and Subsequent Entry Points

The archived record for CGC-001 identifies `template-variables-supply-boundary` as a same-named object whose version needs to be clearly labeled. It addresses the problem of easily confusing referenced objects, not the root cause of this anomaly. After the two same-named objects are separated, each object's corresponding revision and entry-point version still need to be retained alongside the original record.

CGC-017 later confirmed that the object was usable and handed off the forks beyond the current entry point to the maintainer for further handling. What can be confirmed here is that the object now has a usable entry point; this card does not establish which revision was used in this incident, nor the timing of the old entry point's retirement.

The record for CGC-018 preserves the practice of following the execution record to the first broken link and stopping at the results available at that point. It changed the focus of the review: the first broken link is more useful than the last line of green output for preserving the state at the time. The record did not retroactively mark the portion before the broken link as successful, nor did it treat the portion after the stopping point as already completed.

The planned rerun approach for CGC-019 is to keep `template-variables-supply-boundary`, the current entry point, and the command fixed, replacing only the current revision. It matches the anomaly boundary described on this page exactly, but this page contains no rerun results. This action is still a comparison yet to be completed, not a validation conclusion.

The related cards are only used to locate the objects and subsequent entry points. They cannot replace the sequence of events on this page, nor can they be used to fill in the maintainer, version forks, or exit conditions as if these had already been decided.

## Scope of Impact

The impact falls first on template consumers using this entry point: the same entry point cannot reliably represent a single revision, and consumers may receive templates from different sources. The comparison path pointed to a local-path template at one point, showing that the impact was not limited to a change in the page name. A change in the project name may also change the target directory and Template Variables, so recovery cannot consist only of replacing the entry-point text.

The scope of impact did not extend to adjacent services. The record contains no evidence that adjacent projects experienced the same revision mixing, nor any evidence that all templates were affected. Here, "consumers adopting this entry point" is used, and adopters not listed are not described as affected parties.

Caller regression is included in the follow-up diff list, but it has no corresponding pass or fail result. It currently only indicates that the entry-point behavior needs to be reviewed again from the caller side; it cannot indicate that the caller has recovered. The offline-build evidence is likewise incomplete, and green output cannot be used as a substitute.

Changes to the template test command, changes to the generated target directory, and the appearance of placeholder values may all affect the consumer's assessment at the same time, but the existing material does not prove that they occurred together in the same run. The postmortem retains these observations so as not to lose the entry points for later review, rather than stitching them into a single failure chain.

## Why the old wording remains

The old record once stated "Overwriting can restore it." This statement was useful at the time of recovery, but it did not specify which target location was overwritten or whether the same revision was still being used after recovery. We retain this statement now, while limiting it to an observation about recovery.

The old record also put "project-name normalization" first. After it was later discovered that the source selector was still functioning normally, this assessment was weakened, but it was not erased from the historical paragraphs. It represents the earliest working hypothesis available at that time. If readers look only at the latest paragraph, they may mistakenly think that the relationship among the entry point, source, and hook was known from the outset; that does not match the actual record.

Another piece of old text left "why the template test command changed is still unknown" as a blank. That blank still exists. Even though later observations were added about template configuration and Liquid expansion, they cannot fill the gap by treating the test-command difference as evidence that the command was executed or had already failed.

The wording "the current revision of two revisions is placed at the same entry point" also cannot be polished into a more precise version-selection conclusion. The existing material supports only that the entry simultaneously carries two version identifiers; it cannot indicate which version should have overridden which other version, nor whether the mixing occurred during saving, selection, or expansion.

The old ancillary record also retains the terms "favorite entry point," "offline-build evidence," and "caller regression." They are not evidence of equal strength: the first is merely a place to revisit, and the latter two are incomplete materials. Rewriting all three uniformly as completed checks would damage the historical state of this page.

## Boundaries for follow-up review

Follow-up review can start from `template-variables-supply-boundary`: save the two revisions separately, then hold the current entry point and command fixed, changing only revision. Each comparison must retain the source selector's result, whether the local path template was selected, the target directory after project-name normalization, the placeholder values, and the output locations of the pre hook and post hook. This can show which variable, when changed, is accompanied by a change in the observed behavior, but it cannot directly label a single difference as the root cause.

If two revisions appear again at the entry point during follow-up review, first save the original and stop overwriting. If the source selector is still functioning normally, continue comparing the selected template tree; if the result goes into the local path template, record that path and the revision at that time. If the only thing visible is green output before the progress boundary, do not treat it as meaning that the post hook has completed. If the user path has already recovered, still retain the result from before recovery.If the target directory changes because of a project name override, save the old directory and the normalized directory separately; do not combine the two locations into a single "output directory". If Template Variables shows a placeholder value, record the expansion stage at which it appears; there is currently no evidence proving that it must come from the project name, nor any evidence proving that it must come from the revision.

If sub-template is configured, first save the selected subtemplate root, then compare it separately against the parent template tree and the local path template. Do not infer the template root solely from the final output, because the same output may be affected by the project name, source selection, and hooks at the same time. This branch can only help identify what to compare; it cannot close the incident on its own.

If a pre hook or post hook is recorded again, save the output both before and after the progress boundary. If only the preceding section of green output is available, whether the post hook ran remains unknown; if only the subsequent output appears, that also does not allow us to infer that the earlier expansion necessarily used the expected revision. Output order and version identity need to be recorded separately.

The offline build evidence is still incomplete. Caller regression testing also appears only in the subsequent list of differences, with no corresponding pass or fail result. Both can be investigated further, but they cannot be used to add claims about the scope of successful recovery.

## Changes retained between versions

v1 only recorded that the entry point had two revisions, project name normalization differed from earlier records, recovery was possible through overwriting, and changes to the template test command were unclear. It had no timeline and did not separate the source selector from the local path template.

v2 added four relative time points, T+00, T+07, T+18, and T+31, confirming that the template source selector had remained functional and that one result pointed to the local path template. It documented the lack of original input behind the screenshot-based account and separated recovery from root cause confirmation. Template configuration, Liquid expansion, hooks, the generation target directory, and working directory restoration were listed as adjacent observations.

v3 did not remove v2's assessments; instead, it placed the pre hook, post hook, placeholder values, the sub-template root, progress boundaries, caller regression testing, and offline build evidence back in their respective evidentiary contexts. Their appearance side by side does not mean that these observations were all confirmed together in a single run.

v3 also handled source selection and output location separately. Whether the entry point carries two revisions at the same time is a question of object identity; whether the template source selector can still complete its flow is a question of the selection process; the local path template, target directory, and placeholder values are output-side observations. Putting all three in one paragraph can show that they are adjacent, but adjacency must not be presented as causation.

The working assessment that remained at the end was: restoring the user path does not mean that revision boundaries have been confirmed, and confirming that the objects are usable does not mean that the retirement time for the old entry point has been determined. The current entry point can still be used to locate the old state, but this page has not yet established a new, unified position on the scope of adoption, maintenance entry points, and retirement conditions for the two revisions.

## Still unresolved

- How the two objects with the same name in `template-variables-supply-boundary` should each be labeled with their revision.
- Who will continue maintaining the forks downstream of the current entry point, and when the old entry point will be retired.
- With the entry point, commands, and template boundaries fixed, replace only the rerun results for the current revision.
- Whether the template test command actually ran along this path, and whether it affected the output.
- The selection order among the sub-template root, the parent template tree, and the local-path template.
- Whether the screenshot missed any output produced by the post hook after the progress boundary.
- The actual changes to the target directory and placeholder values after project name normalization.
- Evidence from caller regression testing and offline builds.

These items cannot automatically be considered complete just because the user path has been restored. The old entry point and the old version are still being retained so that the next comparison can start from the same state, not to hide unanswered questions behind a recovery result that appears normal.

# On-Call Procedure for a Failed Dependency Boundary Run

## Start

This page covers only one actual run of `template-variables-supply-boundary`. First confirm that the on-call target still belongs to `adj-template-variables`, then open the record from `docs/adj-template-variables/runbooks/template-variables-dependency-boundary-audit-failed-run-on-call-page.md`. Do not attach another run's output to this page or start by substituting a conclusion for the actual run record.

Before starting, record three things: the full command used for this run, the template source the run actually reached, and the generation target directory. If the command or source code needs to change, save the pre-change contents first; judgments on this page depend on the objects seen at runtime, and success cannot be inferred from directory names or default values alone. If the entry file does not match what you see in the run, stop at the entry point, record the path and object you see, then hand it back to that entry point's maintainer.

## Run Sequence

1. **Find the local reference first.** Look for "crate name derivation" in the on-call page above. Follow only that section of the record; do not mix in other projects' Template Variables documentation. If you cannot find that section, stop the run. Do not guess whether the variable comes from the parent template, the child template, or the generation target directory.

2. **Save the first failure.** Check the output from the start of the run in the order it appears. The first time you encounter a failure, a missing file, a path change, or an expected state that does not appear, immediately copy that section of raw output and note beside it which object it corresponds to. Do not start by cleaning up directories or rerunning with multiple sets of parameters, and do not skip the first failure to look at the later "caller regression." Later output may be appended to the same record, but it must not overwrite the first failure.

3. **At the progress boundary.** Do not clear the run state after seeing "progress boundary." It only shows that the run reached that point; on its own, it cannot prove that the template source, variable values, or target directory are correct. Keep the output before and after the boundary, and identify the last object observed and the first object that did not appear afterward; if you cannot distinguish the two, leave the unknowns as they are.

4. **Check caller regression.** If "caller regression" does not appear, stop here. Do not add a success conclusion. Only record it as a later observation if the marker actually appears in the run; even if it appears later, retain the earlier first failure and progress boundary. Do not use the regression marker to override the preceding anomalies.

5. **Change only one condition at a time.** When a recheck is needed, first hold the source code, entry point, and all other command parameters fixed, and change only one explicitly recorded condition. Write each recheck result on a separate line, noting what changed, the first visible change, and whether the run stopped at the same step again. Leave combinations that have not actually been observed blank; do not treat results from adjacent runs as evidence for this run.

## Stop and Roll Back

Stop if any of the following occurs: "crate name derivation" cannot be found; the object or raw output for the first failure was not saved; continuing past "progress boundary" requires clearing the run state; "caller regression" has not appeared but you are already preparing to write a success conclusion; or the entry point in use does not match the record in the file. When you stop, do not widen the investigation or alter the run state just to obtain a full path.

Limit rollback to known restoration actions: keep the old entry point, restore the source code and command records to their pre-change versions, do not delete the failure output, and do not mark unverified recovery actions as completed. The recovery actions have not yet been tried in the shared environment, so the state in the shared environment cannot count as a successful example for this page. If you still cannot confirm the object after rollback, stop at the last visible step.

## Handoff Record

Record the handoff details in the following order next to the corresponding steps on this page:

- Entry point used at the start: `docs/adj-template-variables/runbooks/template-variables-dependency-boundary-audit-failed-run-on-call-page.md`;
- Raw output for the first failure and the object it corresponds to;
- The last section of output retained on each side of "progress boundary";
- Whether "caller regression" appeared;
- The single condition changed, the exit code, and the state still visible after rollback;
- The specific step the next shift needs to resume from, and which combinations remain unverified.

If the record only goes as far as the first failure, stop at the first failure; if only the progress boundary was observed, limit the handoff to that boundary as well. Do not write up "template source selector," the generation target directory, or the sub-template root as a confirmed cause unless the raw output from this run actually links them to the failed object. This on-call page and its attachments are still maintained by `adj-template-variables`; create a new version for later changes rather than overwriting the record of this run.

# Public Entry Maintenance Decision Record

The record for 6 month began with a very narrow dispute: whether the team's public entry should switch directly to the new location during the adjustment window. The meeting did not treat "the entry is still accessible" as proof that the migration had succeeded, nor did it write the expected benefits of the new location as results that had already occurred. The final decision was to retain the current configuration entry for now. This decision addressed the switching risk at the time; it was not a long-term endorsement of the old entry.

## The Two Options on the Table at the Time

Continuing to use the current entry had the most direct benefit of not requiring the team to immediately change its familiar access method, while existing handoff materials could still be found in their original location. The maintenance cost would continue to exist: the old wording would not disappear automatically just because it remained reachable, and people taking over later might read a piece of historical documentation as a complete current description. The review kept this cost in the decision rather than erasing it with the word "stable."

The other option was to switch to the new location during the adjustment window and then organize the entry and handoff materials centrally. Its benefit was only a plan awaiting validation: the materials might be more centralized, and the handoff might be easier to find. The switch itself would also introduce new variables. Callers would need to reconfirm where to enter, what input was actually provided, and when the first result appeared. The meeting had no evidence that the old and new entries carried the same input, nor evidence that the first visible result after the switch would remain unchanged.

Therefore, "switch as soon as the window begins" was not approved. The window could provide time for centralized handling, but it could not by itself become a condition for taking the old entry offline. If the old entry were removed first and a call later failed, the access path, handoff process, and generation flow would all enter investigation at the same time, making it difficult on site to determine where the deviation began. The current entry was retained so that these layers of impact could still be examined separately; this did not classify the new location as infeasible.

## Order of the Review Records

The addendum for 10 month changed the order of recording. First record whether people can enter through the public entry, then the input actually provided by the caller, and finally the first visible result just displayed by the command or call. These three cannot be combined into a single statement that "the path did not change." Entry reachability answers only the access layer and cannot attest to the input content; input that appears identical cannot attest to subsequent results either.

The first result especially cannot be retained only when it is successful. It may be a prompt that appears when the generation flow starts, or it may be a failure that occurs very early. If the change appears after the entry handoff but before the call has started, it should continue to be recorded at the entry site; if the input has already been obtained and the call subsequently fails at cargo-generate, the record should remain at the call site. Both situations may look like "nothing was generated," but they require returning to different places for review.

The successful path is saved separately. If the caller enters through the current entry and sees the generation flow start, that only shows that the old landing point worked up to this step. It does not show that the new entry is ready to take over, nor that later generation results will have no differences. If a later result deviates, continue recording it against that call rather than treating the continued accessibility of the entry as proof of success.

Adjacent failures are also saved separately. When a person cannot obtain content at the entry, first retain the access or handoff phenomenon rather than immediately writing it up as a generation failure; when the input has already been obtained and the failure occurs at cargo-generate, the failure still belongs to the call site. If the first result changes immediately after replacing the entry, stop the switch at that point and reproduce it through the old entry. Temporarily retaining both paths makes it easier to see where the change occurred than compressing the two layers of phenomena into one conclusion.

## Actual Impact Retained by the Decision

The direct impact of continuing to use the current entry is that a familiar public landing point for the team remains available during the adjustment. The coordinator can review the input and first result again from the same location, and the handoff does not have to handle entry replacement and call differences at the same time. The cost is equally clear: the historical wording and new explanations will coexist for a period, and the old materials may still be misread. This arrangement was therefore not written up as "the problem has been solved."

The expected benefit of switching to the new location was to organize the entry and handoff materials centrally and reduce dependence on the old landing point. The review did not treat the expectation as an actual benefit, because at the time no real call could prove that the new location changed the call result, and it had not been confirmed that all callers were ready. The adjustment window can still be used to check these differences, but the date itself does not change the decision.

The discussion repeatedly returned to three specific facts from thepresentfield: where people enter, what input the call carries, and when the first result changes. If entry access is normal but the input record is missing, that cannot be used to approve the switch; if the input is identical but the first result differs, it also cannot be explained simply by saying "the entry did not change." The statement "the path did not change" in the old record was too broad; the addendum for 10 month only broke it down and did not claim that all subsequent impacts had been investigated.

The meeting materials required the actual impact, the coordinator, and a reversible old entry to be recorded. The coordinator currently confirmed is Chen Siyuan. Long-term ownership, a unified switch date, and the migration status of all callers, where unsupported by the materials, have still not been written as facts. People participating in the review may add the call or handoff materials they actually obtained, but that will not automatically change the subject of this round's decision.

## Retained Earlier Opinions

"Switch during the window first, then organize the entry centrally" remains in the old record. It expresses a preference for centralized handling, not an already approved switching step. If this sentence were rewritten as the current process, readers would assume that the new location, input, and first result had already been confirmed to correspond directly. Its original tendency is retained here, with the unresolved on-site issues noted beside it.

The objection that keeping the old entry available will extend the period during which historical wording coexists has also not been deleted. It cannot be offset by calling it a "stable landing point," nor will it disappear automatically because the adjustment window has begun. New content should be placed in the handoff record, while the old entry continues to serve review and rollback purposes; this decision did not expand the old documentation into a new complete guide.

Earlier materials also left a broader judgment: the entry did not change, and therefore the call path did not change. That judgment was sufficient at the time to support postponing the switch, but it was narrowed in the 10 month review. The entry, input, and first result may each change independently, so the entry status can no longer represent the entire call path. The old judgment is retained to explain why the switch was not made immediately at the time; the narrowed record explains that it now covers only the entry layer.

## Diagram and On-Site Usage

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[Current configuration entry] --> B[Caller input]
  B --> C[First visible result]
  D[Adjustment window] --> E[New location]
  E --> B
  A --> F[Reversible old entry]
```

The order in the diagram is the recording method adopted for subsequent reviews, not a process that had already been clearly written in 6 month. The diagram places the adjustment window before the new location to show that the window provides an opportunity for handling; it does not mean that switching is mandatory when the time arrives. The old entry points to a reversible landing point, which does not mean that two sets of entries must always be maintained simultaneously; it indicates that there is still an option to return to the original location if the switch fails.

If a review obtains only a result showing that entry access is normal, it can be recorded only in the entry box. Without the corresponding input and first result, it cannot be upgraded to approval for the switch. If the result obtained is an adjacent failure at the entry, first retain the old entry and record where it occurred; if it is a failure after the input has been handed to cargo-generate, continue checking it at the call site. The record may temporarily look untidy this way, but failures from different locations will not be mixed together.

If the default landing point is to be reevaluated later, it must at least be possible to correlate the entry, input, and first result to the same call, and the switch must still be reversible. Here, "reversible" means that the old entry has not been discarded first; it is not an abstract long-term commitment. The current materials provide neither a unified switch date nor evidence that all callers have completed migration, so this version does not add either item.

## Decision in This Version

The current configuration entry will continue as the team's public landing point, the adjustment window will not trigger an automatic switch, and the old entry will be retained as a rollback point. Maintenance records begin with a real cargo-generate call and describe the entry, input, and first visible result separately; entry reachability does not substitute for generation success, and a failure during generation is not written back as an entry failure.

This decision did not change the call semantics of cargo-generate, nor did it approve new long-term ownership of the entry. For handoff continuity after entry replacement, see also DOC-44. If the next review still has only the entry status and lacks the input and first result from the same call, this record remains at the decision to retain the current entry.

# Shared Entry-Point Maintenance Deviation Postmortem

This deviation occurred during a maintenance window for the team's shared entry point. When the window ended, the entry was still visible, but the result visitors saw did not match the original plan. The on-site record first separated "entry accessible" from "maintenance result correct"; at that point, the only impact that could be confirmed was to the visible content of the shared entry point. Whether the generation command or other projects were affected was not confirmed then.

## Incident timeline

- During the maintenance window: The shared entry point was handled according to the original plan, but the process record was incomplete.
- First discovered: The check result did not match expectations. Further changes were paused, and the CLI output on the on-call terminal was retained.
- Temporary response: The entry was restored to an accessible state. The restoration occurred within the window, but there is no minute-level timestamp and no evidence that the root cause had been identified.
- During the postmortem: Gao Yan helped organize the impact and coordination details, while Zheng Wei preserved the anomaly observed on site. They treated "maintenance completed" and "result verified" as two separate states.

The raw output excerpt retained at the time under CLI is below; the original terminal text was not fully backfilled:

> CLI Raw output excerpt: `The visible result did not match the original plan`

This excerpt proves only that the deviation was seen on site; it does not prove where the divergence occurred. The initial assessment was that this was a display discrepancy during the maintenance window. Later material was still insufficient to confirm or overturn that assessment, so the earlier wording is retained here rather than being written as an attribution to a specific component. The affected entry's access method, the order of the maintenance actions, and the actual content displayed before and after restoration were not saved item by item at the time.

## Controls retained in the postmortem

The record was supplemented with three things that had been documented too vaguely during the shift: the actual impact, the coordinator, and the old entry that could be rolled back. The old entry was not deleted after the temporary restoration; it remained as a rollback option. In the next similar window, first verify what visitors actually see, then decide whether to roll back or continue adjusting; "restored" alone is not enough to judge that maintenance is complete.

Still unconfirmed: exactly which action caused the divergence between the original plan and the final display; whether the CLI output corresponds to the entry itself or the result returned after maintenance; and whether the temporary restoration changed the preconditions for a subsequent window. Until these records exist, do not attribute this incident to a specific component or treat a single temporary restoration as a permanent fix.

Addendum: During the next window, the on-call person will save a screenshot of the entry and the original command text at the same time, for comparison between the two states.

# On-Call Procedure for Shared Entry-Point Maintenance

When a message about Team Shared Entry-Point Maintenance comes in, first save the version of rhai-hooks, the unprocessed results, and the downstream crate compilation results; do not change configuration first or replace the raw output with a failure summary.

The handoff must include the invocation method, the template source, the execution version, and a reproducible result. At the first divergence into configuration, Git, or hook internals, hand it to the corresponding maintainer; the on-call person keeps only entry-point-side records.

Stop immediately if this requires expanded permissions, changing public behavior, or deciding scope on behalf of the long-term owner.

# Shared Entry Point Maintenance Results Troubleshooting Tree

A ticket says "team shared entry point maintenance" is complete, but the results still can't be verified. First ask for the call entry point and version for `template-rendering`.

```text
Ticket marked complete
└─ Entry point and version?
   ├─ Either missing: stop; find someone who can confirm
   └─ Both available: compare paired call records for the same input
      ├─ Mismatch: stop at the difference; record the actual impact
      └─ Match but results differ: confirm the coordinator and whether the old entry point can be withdrawn
```

Who takes over when the two sides don't match has not been documented yet.
